## The core purpose (read this before making any scope trade-off)

This is not a generic nutrition tracker. The primary job: help someone with an autoimmune condition relearn how and what to eat, and understand — personally, for their own body — how food affects them. Hashimoto's thyroiditis was the first condition built out to full depth, and the one nearly every existing feature and citation below is written for as of this document's own earlier history — the direction, decided 2026-08-08 and restated even more explicitly by the person later the same day, is genuinely broader, not a lesser-effort broadening either: **"this is no longer just focused on Hashimoto's, it is focused on all 19 both individually and if a person has multiple of them combined. The scope of this app is not longer just to perfect it for Hashimoto's. The scope is to perfect it for all of the others, too."** Every one of the 18 non-Hashimoto's conditions is a real, standing target for the same ~176-entry depth Hashimoto's itself has, not a lesser tier that structural parity alone satisfies — see the Status section's own "volumetric depth push" entries for where this stands numerically at any given time. Real, combined-condition (polyautoimmunity) management is its own named, standing scope item too, not yet built as a first-class browsable destination — see the same Status entries for the honest state of that specific piece. Meal building, shopping lists, and scheduling are scaffolding that make daily use sustainable enough to generate that understanding; they are not the point on their own. When in doubt about priority, favor whatever helps someone discover and act on their own personal food-effect patterns over convenience features.

**Gut/microbiome healing is an explicit, named goal**, not just a side effect of good food choices — the app is also meant to actively help repair the person's microbiome and gut health, not just help them choose foods that avoid triggering symptoms.

**Refined framing (user's own words):** the real-world problem is that people are overwhelmed and confused about food, and most of them can't put the pieces together themselves the way a motivated, detail-oriented person might. The app's job is to remove that cognitive burden entirely — do the correlation/discovery work *for* the person, so day-to-day eating becomes a matter of following clear, pre-solved rules ("play by the rules of food, chemistry, etc.") rather than an ongoing research project. The complexity (matching foods to body chemistry, catching interactions, finding personal patterns) should live inside the app and its rules engine; what the person experiences should be ease — a grocery list that's already built for them, a plate that's already been figured out, so they can become the healthiest version of themselves without having to become their own nutritionist first. This reframes discovery/trend-finding as something the app does on the user's behalf, not a task handed to them.

**Home cooking over commercial/branded products, decided 2026-08-04.** Explicit product direction, given while discussing whether soups belong in `Mixed`: the app should promote actually cooking from real ingredients, not leaning on store-bought branded/commercial products as the default path. The person should be able to save their own real builds for things they make themselves — which the Food tab's ten builders (Meal, Side, Salad, Smoothie, Fermentation, Beverage, Snack, Baked Goods, Soup, Sauces) already do, each saving a genuine standalone record assembled from raw reference-database ingredients, not a generic branded pick. If someone wants to log a specific store-bought/branded product, the intended path is scanning it in (the still-unbuilt barcode/product-scan feature already named in Next Steps), not picking a generic "commercial"/"préemballée" reference-database entry standing in for it. Practical implication for the reference database work itself: don't expand or lean further into "commercial"/branded reference entries going forward, and treat the ones already in the database (heavily present across sources, e.g. France_Ciqual's many "..., préemballée" rows, Australia_AFCD's "..., commercial" rows) as a stand-in for the not-yet-built scan feature rather than the intended long-term path -- worth remembering when a future pass touches any category still mixing homemade-style entries with commercial ones.

**International scope, decided 2026-08-08 — the app is not US-centric, and every one of the 19 conditions needs real, cited, country/region-specific evidence, not just US data.** Direct, explicit statement from the app's creator, quoted verbatim since it's a real, standing pivot the same way the "all 19 conditions" statement above was: "I want this to look at all of the evidence for the whole planet and be able to report statistics based on country or general area. this should be avilable in all 19 conditions related to it specifically. Provide the corroborating evidence for the reasons they are having these problems in their countries, just as we are for the US, and make the app no[t] contric [centric] to the US. We are reaching out to the world to all that are affected, not just those in the US. This will be an international app, and will be in several different languages." Three real, distinct components, not one task:

1. **Real, cited international/regional epidemiological data per condition** — how prevalence, incidence, and severity vary by country or region, for all 19 conditions, not just the US population most of this app's existing research has implicitly centered. A first real batch of this — one dedicated "Global Perspective" entry per condition, covering both the real regional prevalence data AND the real, cited corroborating explanation for why (genetics, diet, environment, latitude, healthcare/screening practices, industrialization) — started the same day; see the Status section's own dated entry for exactly which conditions are covered so far. This is real, substantial, ongoing research work, comparable in scope to the volumetric-depth-push already underway, not a single-pass task.
2. **A real, decided-but-not-yet-built internationalization (i18n) architecture** — the actual language list, stated directly by the app's creator: all common English variants (US, UK, AU, and others), Spanish (both Latin American and Spain's own variant), German, French, Finnish, Norwegian, Swedish, and Japanese. **Chinese and Italian removed from this list, 2026-08-10, direct instruction** ("Remove Chinese and Italian as a languages that will be available") -- the same day's own international-food-source research had already found real, practical reasons both were going to be genuinely harder than the rest (mainland China had no real open-data food-composition portal, only a substitute via Taiwan; Italy's own free source was search-only with no bulk export, and its paid alternative wasn't free), and the person's own direct call was to drop both rather than pursue either. No i18n library is wired into this app yet (no `expo-localization`, no `react-i18next` or equivalent, no string-extraction pass has been done across any screen) — this is real, substantial engineering work: picking the technical approach, extracting every user-facing string across dozens of screens, wiring locale detection and a real language-switcher, and only then actually translating. Deliberately not started as code this same day — a token, half-wired i18n library with two translated strings would misrepresent real progress on a task this large, the same discipline this document already holds cloud sync and household sharing to.
3. **Country-specific reference data** — the app already has real, existing infrastructure directly relevant to this goal, worth naming so it isn't rebuilt from scratch: the 22,022-food nutrition reference database already draws from 7 real national sources (USDA/US, Canada's CNF, the UK's CoFID, Germany's BLS, Australia's AFCD, France's Ciqual, and Japan's MEXT) — meaning the food-data layer already has real, direct coverage for the US, UK, Australian, Canadian, French, German, and Japanese populations named in the language list above. Real gaps against the current (post-removal) language list: no Spanish-speaking country's own national food-composition data yet, and no Nordic (Finnish/Norwegian/Swedish) source yet -- both actively being closed, see the Status section's own dated entry for the real import-pipeline work in progress.

**Real, honest scoping**: this is a genuinely large, multi-session initiative on the same order as the original nutrition-database build or the ongoing volumetric-depth-push, not something completed in one pass. The plan going forward: keep adding real, cited Global Perspective content per condition (Phase 1, in progress); make a real, deliberate i18n technical-architecture decision and build the underlying plumbing (Phase 2, not started); translate the app's own UI strings (Phase 3, not started); and decide + execute a real content-translation strategy for the Digest's own now-900+-entry research library across 10+ languages — likely requiring either a professional translation service integration or a carefully-scoped machine-translation approach, a real, undecided design question in its own right (Phase 4, not started).

## Architecture decisions made

*None of the cloud-backup, sync, encryption, or household-sharing architecture described in this section has been implemented yet — all app code so far is local-only, single-device (see Status above). This section remains the decided plan for when that work starts.*

**Local-first, no company server holding health data.** The live/authoritative database lives on the primary account holder's device. There is no backend server storing anyone's health data — full stop. This is a deliberate trust/privacy stance, not just a technical choice.

**Encrypted backup to the user's own cloud drive.** The primary device periodically writes an encrypted backup/snapshot to a folder in the user's own OneDrive/Google Drive/etc. (their account, their storage). This backup serves two purposes: disaster recovery, and (see below) transport for household sharing. The backup is not a readable file without importing it back into the app.

**Recovery model, chosen deliberately.** Encryption is protected by a master password or a locally-generated recovery key shown to the user once during setup (the same pattern password managers use). The app never holds the user's key — meaning there is intentionally no "forgot password" flow. This is the accepted cost of a genuine zero-knowledge design, not an oversight.

**Platform scope (revised): Android, iPhone, Windows, and Mac.** The app is no longer mobile-only — it needs to be usable from all four.

**Desktop technology — decided.** Expo already supports a "web" build target (via React Native Web), built on the same codebase as the mobile app — no separate toolchain needed. This web build is configured as an installable PWA (Progressive Web App): the UI and most business logic are shared with mobile; the local storage layer needs a platform-specific implementation (browser IndexedDB instead of on-device SQLite), and any native-only modules need web equivalents.

- **Windows**: full traditional "install from the Microsoft Store" experience, via PWABuilder packaging the PWA into an MSIX for Store submission. Zero platform fee — Microsoft eliminated individual developer registration fees in September 2025, and extended free registration to company accounts as well as of a Windows Developer Blog post in May 2026.
- **Mac**: installable PWA, not listed in the Mac App Store. This deliberately avoids Apple's Developer Program fee ($99/year, recurring, required for Mac App Store distribution regardless of framework) and its notarization/review process — a PWA installed via the browser's own "Add to Dock"/install mechanism never enters Apple's app-signing pipeline at all, unlike a traditionally distributed native binary (e.g., an Electron-wrapped app), which would still need notarization even outside the App Store to avoid Gatekeeper warnings. Revisit only if a future need for full Mac App Store presence outweighs the ongoing fee.

**Multi-device sync & control model (the person's own devices).** Refined from an earlier "one primary device is authoritative" framing into a cleaner, symmetric model: the encrypted cloud-backup folder (same location already described below) is the actual current state, not just a disaster-recovery copy. A device pulls the latest encrypted snapshot, decrypts it locally with the master password/key, and works with that as its own live local database from that point — preserving full offline capability, since the cloud only needs to be reachable at the pull/push transition points, not during everyday use (logging a meal with no signal still works). When done, the device pushes an updated encrypted snapshot back. This one mechanism now does three jobs: disaster-recovery backup, syncing between the same person's own phone/Windows/Mac, and the transport for household companion sharing described below (with the companion's access scope restricted, versus full access for the primary user's own devices).

Three layered safety mechanisms prevent two devices from editing the same data at once, fastest/most common to slowest/most rare:

1. *Locking ("control")*: whichever device pulls the database first holds exclusive control, recorded in the cloud metadata. A commit does not release control by itself — control persists until the app is closed, the screen times out/locks, or (if the person doesn't use a screen lock) an inactivity timer detects the app sitting open and idle in the foreground.
2. *Active takeover*: from a second device, the person taps a "take over/connect" button. This sends a *visible*, tap-required push notification to the controlling device — deliberately not a silent background push, since silent pushes are documented as best-effort and can be delayed or dropped by iOS/Android background throttling, while visible notifications are delivered far more reliably (that's the core job a notification system is built to do). The requesting device's screen names the controlling device by name (e.g., "Your iPhone currently has control") and instructs the person to check the notification there. Tapping that notification runs a background action that commits current local state and releases control; on iOS/Android the app then drops into a locked, read-only "this session moved to your other device" screen (apps can't force-quit themselves on mobile OSes the way a desktop program can; on Windows/Mac the app can cleanly exit itself, which is normal there). If the controlling device doesn't respond within roughly 1-2 minutes (a human needs to notice and tap, not an instant background process), the requesting device offers "take control anyway" — showing exactly how stale the other device's last save was (e.g., "iPhone last saved 2 hours ago") so the person makes an informed, explicit choice about what might be lost, rather than a silent automatic override.
3. *Stale-lock expiration*: a hard maximum lease of 30 minutes on control, independent of the graceful signals above — if no renewal happens in that window (crashed app, dead battery, lost/stolen device, permanent connectivity loss), control auto-expires regardless, so a single unreachable device can never permanently lock the person out of their own data.

Underneath all three, last-write-wins plus a visible activity log remains as the final safety net for whatever narrow edge cases slip past the above (e.g., cloud-sync propagation delay letting two devices briefly both believe they hold control) — the same conflict policy already used for household companion sync below, reused rather than inventing a second system. This design deliberately reuses two pieces already decided elsewhere in this document: the minimal content-blind push relay (APNs/FCM) originally built for reminders' cross-device nudges is the same signal used for takeover notifications, and the "show your own freshness/confidence" principle originally built for reminders is reused for the "last saved X ago" risk disclosure during a forced takeover.

**Household sharing, two access tiers, both reading from a shared cloud folder:**
- *Free viewer companion*: the primary shares their cloud backup folder (via the cloud provider's own native folder-sharing, not a custom mechanism) to a second person. That person's app reads periodic snapshots from the shared folder — modeled on how Anki's "shared decks" feature works (one-way, periodic reimport that merges in new content without wiping the viewer's own local state; no live subscription/auto-update exists in Anki either, and that absence is fine here too). The viewer can see the meal schedule, shopping list, and trend reports, and query details — but cannot edit most things.
- *One narrow exception*: the viewer CAN check off shopping list items. This is treated as a distinct, safe category of "write-back" — idempotent, single-field, low-conflict-risk actions (checking off a list item, marking a scheduled task complete) — sent back to the primary as a small delta/answer file. This is different in kind from full write access, and deliberately so: no general merge logic is needed for this category.
- *Paid interactive companion*: real read-write access to a shared "household domain" (meal plan, shopping list, schedule) — but NOT to the primary's "personal health domain" (symptom logs, labs, supplements, their own scoring/trend history), which stays owned by the primary and unreachable by any companion account, even the paid one. This split exists for both security and product-trust reasons.
- *Conflict handling for the interactive tier*: last-write-wins per field, plus a visible activity log so nothing silently disappears ("Alex removed milk at 4:12pm, overriding your edit from 4:10pm"). This is intentionally not a heavyweight CRDT/merge system — validated by the fact that AnkiWeb's own mature, decades-refined sync still falls back to a full one-way overwrite when changes genuinely can't merge (e.g., structural changes). Revisit only if real usage shows last-write-wins isn't good enough.
- *Cross-provider question, resolved 2026-08-08*: household sharing does **not** require both people to use the same cloud provider — confirmed directly. The real sync mechanism that makes a Partner/Guardian/Caregiver relationship work when each side backs up to a different provider (OneDrive on one end, Google Drive on the other) is deliberately still deferred to a later, dedicated design pass, not solved here.

**Reminders/scheduling, contextual from day one (not clock-based).** A reminder like "take your levothyroxine" should account for what's actually been logged — e.g., warn that a calcium-rich food logged earlier pushes the safe window later — not just fire at a fixed preset time. This splits into two different mechanisms:
- Fully local, on-device scheduled notifications (no server) for anything self-contained and recomputed instantly whenever the user is actively using the app.
- A minimal, content-blind push relay (APNs/FCM) only for cross-device nudges ("the other person just changed something") — this is a real server component, but it never carries actual health content, only a wake-up signal.
- Real mobile OS constraint: background execution is throttled on both iOS and Android, so "recompute the moment something changes" is only guaranteed while the app is in the foreground; background recomputation is best-effort on the OS's own refresh schedule, not instant. Design around this rather than assuming perfect real-time background updates.
- Reminders should show their own confidence/freshness (e.g., "based on food logged as of 7:45am") so the user can tell when contextual guidance might be based on stale data — because a late-logged contextual reminder can be confidently wrong, which is arguably worse than a dumb static reminder being honestly uninformed.

**Interaction rules engine — two kinds, both available from day one, kept visually distinct:**
- *Built-in, cited rules*: prescription/supplement/food timing interactions (e.g., levothyroxine + calcium/iron absorption interference, biotin interfering with certain thyroid lab assays) — authored with the same real-citation discipline as the nutrition database (FDA labeling, endocrinology guidance, pharmacology literature), not assumed/common-knowledge rules. Distinct research effort from the existing D1-D6 food scoring. Should probably ship as a maintainable, versioned data file/ruleset that can update independently of app releases, similar to how antivirus/spam-filter rule updates work.
- *Personal rule builder*: lets the individual user encode their own discovered pattern or their own doctor's specific instruction to them (which might differ from the general guideline). Must be labeled distinctly from the cited rules so personal hypothesis is never confused with verified medical fact, including in any doctor-facing report.
- *Synergy to build toward*: the trend engine should be able to surface candidate personal rules from observed patterns ("you've logged fatigue within a day of high-goitrogen meals four times this month — want to turn that into a reminder?"), closing the loop between passive tracking and actionable personal knowledge.

**Late/retroactive logging**: must be allowed and low-friction — guided quick-select questions rather than a blank form (what did you eat/take → quick-select from favorites/recents → when did it actually happen → smart time picker). Every late entry should immediately show its consequence (recalculated schedule impact), turning logging into a small teaching moment rather than a chore. Scheduled reminders should double as catch-up checkpoints ("anything since we last talked?") rather than relying on the user to self-initiate a late entry.

## Monetization — tiers

**Expanded to five real priced tiers plus one bundled role, 2026-08-08**, superseding the original two-tier sketch below it (written back when the app had a single meal builder and one condition; both are stale on their own terms now, not just narrow). Refined further the same day once real pricing and four open design questions got resolved. Full reasoning, a feature-access matrix, and the pricing framework behind each number is in the [Household & Monetization Tiers Artifact](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/e153d351-52c7-4df5-a4c1-e134ff86c085); this is the short version:

- **Free** (0x, $0): all eleven food builders; Insights limited to the Food Lookup lens only (single-food nutrition facts, no condition scoring); Schedule limited to Meals/Hydration/Exercise (no Supplements/Prescriptions/Doctor Appointments); Trends limited to exercise only; no Signals, no Reports, no interaction-rules engine, no household sharing. Purple Digest itself is not available — Free sees **"Food Basics"** instead, a real, differently-iconed (not the purple ribbon) tab covering only the Digest's genuinely general-knowledge categories (proposed starting split: Food Additives, Food Industry & History, Nutrient Interactions, Mitochondria & Metabolism, Complementary Therapies, Glossary — roughly a third of the current 18, final entry-by-entry tagging deferred to implementation). The same tab re-brands to "Purple Digest" in place on upgrade, not a second feature.
- **Individual** ($9.99/mo, $89.99/yr, the 1.0x base unit): everything Free lacks — full condition-specific scoring for every condition selected in Profile, the full interaction-rules engine, Trends, Reports, the full Schedule, the complete Purple Digest, sync across every device the person themselves owns. One person, their own data only.
- **Partner** ($14.99/mo, $134.99/yr for both — ~1.5x, not 2.0x): two people, each with full Individual-level access to their own data, plus granular, opt-in, per-category visibility into each other's (meals/shopping default shared; symptoms/labs/notes default private; medications a named explicit choice at setup) — a genuinely different, symmetric relationship from the household model below, not an extension of it.
- **Household / Family** (free for the first 2-3 seats, then $1.99/mo, $17.99/yr per seat, ~0.2x): the original "free viewer companion" concept, now with real per-seat economics attached (anchored to Calm's/Headspace's own real family-plan math) — read access to the shared meal plan/shopping list/Trends summary, one narrow write exception (shopping-list checkoffs, marking a scheduled task done), no visibility into the subscriber's personal health domain, no scoring of their own.
- **Guardian** ($0, bundled with Individual/Partner, per child): new, distinct from Caregiver below — a parent's own minor children only. Real, full condition tracking (medications, symptoms, doctor appointments, labs), turned on per category by the parent, who always retains full read/write access; the child's own direct access is separately and granularly configured (from zero self-interaction up to near-full self-service), entirely at the parent's own pace. Legally simpler than Caregiver's own consent problem, since a parent/guardian already has ordinary authority over a minor's health decisions.
- **Caregiver** ($4.99/mo, $49.99/yr per cared-for person, ~0.55x): real write access to another person's meals, medications, symptoms, and schedule on their behalf — not a viewer role, and explicitly **not** for a parent's own minor children (that's Guardian above). For aging parents, other relatives, or professional/independent caregiving. Requires the cared-for person's own explicit consent when they have the capacity to give it; when they don't, the app provides the technical capability and a plain attestation step, deliberately deferring the real legal/guardianship question rather than arbitrating it in-product. Built to work even when the cared-for person has no device or account of their own at all. Stackable on top of any other tier a caregiver already holds for their own use.
- **Addon tiers, later**: sleep tracking, exercise tracking, lab result tracking/trending, and other future health-tracking features layer on as paid addons, unchanged from the original plan.

**Cross-provider sharing, resolved 2026-08-08**: Partner, Guardian, and Caregiver relationships do **not** require both sides to use the same cloud backup provider. The real sync mechanism that makes this work across providers is deliberately still deferred to a later, dedicated design pass.

**Original two-tier sketch, kept for its own historical record**: Free was originally scoped as "single meal builder, general nutritional info only, no Hashimoto's 6-dimension scoring, no reporting, no trends" — accurate before the ten-builder Food tab existed. The original paid tier bundled "meal builder + shopping list, trends, the full 6-dimension scoring, the daily schedule with contextual reminders, doctor reporting, household sharing (both companion tiers), and cloud backup" as one flat tier, with the household economics decision that a companion seat should be a separate, cheaper seat rather than a second full-price subscription — a decision the Household/Family tier above keeps, just with a real number attached.

## Reporting

Doctor/nutritionist/trainer/self reports are different views over the same underlying time-stamped, taggable log data — designed so every log entry is timestamped and taggable from the start, since reporting becomes a query rather than a rebuild if the schema supports it from day one. Reports generate entirely on-device (PDF export, no server rendering) — consistent with the stated privacy model that the only data ever leaving the device is something the user explicitly exports/prints/emails themselves.

## Technology stack — decided

- **Framework: React Native, built on Expo.** Chosen over Flutter specifically because this project needs heavy third-party integration (OneDrive, Google Drive, push notifications, app store billing, encrypted local storage), and React Native's package ecosystem has broader off-the-shelf coverage for that kind of work — meaningful for a solo builder.
- **Why Expo specifically**: the user's dev hardware is a Windows PC + Android phone, no Mac (daughter has an iPhone, available for occasional testing only). Expo Go lets the user run the app live on their own Android phone during development with no Mac and no native build step. When a real installable build is needed later (including iOS), Expo's cloud build service (EAS Build) compiles it on Expo's servers — a Mac is never required, even for shipping to the App Store.
- **Builder's background**: 30 years as an IT Manager, "some scripting/basics" hands-on coding experience, no prior mobile app development, but a strong track record of learning new technical domains as needed. Building this themselves with ongoing step-by-step direction and code-level help from Claude Code in VS Code, not handing it to a separate developer.
- **First milestone: complete.** The "Hello World" toolchain validation (Node.js, VS Code, Expo tooling, Expo Go on the Android phone) succeeded and was superseded by real feature development starting 2026-07-19 — see Status above.

## Technology directions discussed (not yet finalized beyond the above)

- Cross-platform mobile framework — decided, see above.
- On-device storage: SQLite (matches the existing nutrition database format already), likely encrypted at rest via something like SQLCipher; envelope encryption pattern for the master-password/recovery-key model.
- Cloud backup integration: Microsoft Graph API (OneDrive) and Google Drive API, using each provider's app-specific-folder support.
- Push notifications: APNs (iOS) + FCM (Android) for the cross-device nudge signal only.
- Subscriptions/entitlements: Apple StoreKit + Google Play Billing for payment processing (required by platform policy), plus a small entitlement-check backend — the one honest exception to "no server," since it holds billing/tier metadata only, never health data.
- On-device PDF generation libraries for reporting/export.

Real, independently-verified findings added: CKD's real dialysis-diet reversal (the pre-dialysis protein-restriction and potassium-limiting rules often flip once dialysis starts, since dialysis itself removes protein and fluid/potassium restrictions often intensify instead — NIDDK); MASLD's PNPLA3 I148M gene variant (a real 2.76x fatty-liver-odds / 4.44x MASH-odds increase per copy, a genuine gene-environment interaction with alcohol/obesity/T2D — MedlinePlus Genetics); Type 2 Diabetes's dawn phenomenon vs. Somogyi effect (two real, distinct causes of high morning blood sugar requiring a real 2-3AM testing protocol to tell apart, with CGM-era research finding the Somogyi rebound less common than once assumed — PMID 21717414); IBS's real SIBO-overlap caveat (72% positive on the lactulose breath test vs. 36-46% on the glucose test, with a real, direct methodological flaw explaining the gap, and a real, honest finding that test positivity didn't reliably correlate with symptom severity — PMC10134763); Migraine's real, underrecognized vestibular subtype (roughly 1% of the general population, up to 73% of migraine-with-aura patients meeting real criteria, with real underrecognition data showing only 20% of patients volunteer the symptom unprompted vs. 75% when asked directly — PMID 38619053); Cardiovascular Disease's real CANTOS trial (a pure anti-inflammatory drug, canakinumab, reduced real cardiovascular events with zero cholesterol change at all, the first phase 3 proof that inflammation is a real, independently treatable cardiovascular driver — NEJM, PMID 28845751); Gout's real diuretic-driven prescribing cascade (a real, large case-control study found diuretics carry a roughly 2.5-fold gout risk overall, loop+thiazide combined use nearly doubling that again to 4.65-fold, a real, concrete example of this app's own already-built prescribing-cascade concept — PMID 24449584); and Prostate Health's real Harvard ejaculation-frequency finding (a real, 18-year, 31,925-man study found 21+ monthly ejaculations tracking with a real 31% lower prostate cancer risk, holding up after adjusting for PSA-screening frequency specifically — Harvard Health Publishing).

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean across the whole project) and `npx eslint` on every touched file — clean. **Four real batches now landed in one day (75 new entries across all 18 non-Hashimoto's conditions)** — this is the first day every condition has received at least one volumetric-depth batch, still real, honest, incremental progress, not completion: every condition remains well under 55 entries against Hashimoto's own 176. Only Psoriasis hasn't had its own dedicated volumetric batch (it stayed at 20 while MS moved ahead this round) — the natural next pick whenever this resumes. **Not yet exercised on-device.**

**A real Digest layout/UX pass began the same day, following a Google-search-sourced knowledge-base-design brief the person shared and asked to discuss.** Rather than adopt every recommendation uncritically, each suggestion was checked against what's actually built (`app/(tabs)/purple-digest.tsx`, `components/LensHub.tsx`) before deciding what to build: several were already effectively satisfied (related-entry chips already exist via `relatedIds`; the whole Digest is a bundled TS array, so "offline access" was already structurally true; full-text search already matches symptom words in prose). Four real, low-risk wins were picked to build first, explicitly deferring the two genuinely large asks (tracked-data "Pattern Reminders," a Direct-to-Tracker action button, both requiring cross-tab integration into Bio-Compass/Schedule) as their own separate, deliberate future initiative rather than folding them in blind.

**Win 1 -- a real, persistent search bar.** Previously "Search All" was one of ~21 tiles you had to open LensHub and tap into first. A new search input now sits permanently at the top of the screen (a real sibling of `SwipeableTabScreen`, not nested inside `GatedTabContent`'s own children, which render nothing at all until `revealed` -- the bar has to live outside that gate to be usable before any lens has ever been picked). Typing switches straight into the existing `'search'` lens and reveals the screen if it hasn't been already, writing into the same `searchQuery` state the lens's own content already reads -- a second way to populate one state, not a second search mechanism. The old in-content search input inside the `'search'` lens branch was removed as the now-redundant duplicate it would have become.

**Win 2 -- the person's own tracked conditions are pinned to the top of the LensHub picker, using data that already existed and was already unused for this purpose.** `getUserConditions()` (built earlier the same day's own multi-condition work, previously only read by Profile) is now fetched on every focus and used to reorder `LENSES`: Basic Health always leads, then every condition the person has actually selected (in their own already-established build order), then everything else -- real, fewer taps to reach a condition someone actually tracks, without hiding or removing anything else. A leading "★ " marks a matched tile's own grid label so the reorder has a visible, explained reason, not an unexplained shuffle. Required a real, hand-verified mapping (`CONDITION_CODE_TO_DIGEST_KEY`) between the `conditions` reference table's own snake_case codes and this screen's camelCase `DigestCategoryKey` -- confirmed directly against the live database via `sqlite3.exe` rather than guessed, since a wrong mapping would have silently failed to match anything.

**Win 3 -- every condition category (not just Basic Health) now uses the same real shelf-row-plus-detail-panel UI, organized into 4 real pillars, instead of one long flat accordion list.** This is the largest and riskiest of the four wins, a genuine behavioral change to how all 19 conditions (Hashimoto's included) are browsed. Rather than store a new field on 840 existing entries (a real content-authoring undertaking, not a UI change), pillar assignment is computed at render time from a heuristic reading each entry's own `id` and title, the same "reasonable v1, computed not stored" precedent already established by `BASIC_HEALTH_GROUPS`' own id-prefix matching and the food-name-grouping feature elsewhere in this app. Four pillars: Core Science, Self-Advocacy & Testing, Whole-Body Effects, History & Life Stages -- each condition's own real closing "tying-together" synthesis entry is pulled out of the shelves entirely and shown as its own standalone "Putting It Together" card below them, since it summarizes across the whole category rather than fitting one pillar.

**The classifier was validated against all 840 real entries before shipping, not assumed correct** -- a real Node script (mirroring the actual regex logic) run against every condition file surfaced two genuine misclassifications on the first pass: an "-overview" entry landing in "Whole-Body Effects" because its own title named body systems directly (MS's own overview literally says "brain and spinal cord"), and a real priority-order bug where a pregnancy entry's own title containing the word "diagnosed" caused it to match the (weaker, title-text-driven) self-advocacy check before ever reaching the (stronger, deliberately-named-by-this-app's-own-id-convention) pregnancy/stages check. Both fixed: `-overview` entries are now forced to Core Science outright before any other check runs, and the id-based stages check now runs before the title-text-driven advocacy check. Re-validated against all 840 entries afterward with zero remaining known misclassifications.

A real, latent bug in the underlying scroll mechanism was also caught and fixed while building this: `groupRefs` (keyed by plain group-label strings like "Core Science") is shared across every condition, and since every condition now has its own "Core Science" shelf, a stale ref left over from whichever category was open before a lens switch could theoretically be scrolled to for one frame before the new category's real shelf mounted and overwrote it. Fixed by resetting `groupRefs.current = {}` on every lens switch (both `LensHub`'s own `onSelect` and `jumpToRelated`), eliminating the collision risk structurally rather than trying to make every label globally unique.

**Win 4 -- a reading-time estimate and cross-condition tag pills, both computed from data this app already has, no new content authored.** `estimateReadingMinutes()` is a plain word-count-over-200wpm calculation on the same body text already shown when a card expands. `crossConditionCategories()` reuses each entry's already-existing `relatedIds` to surface, as small, deliberately non-tappable pills, which OTHER conditions a given entry's own Related list reaches into -- deliberately not a second tap target, since `RelatedChips` (already rendered further down the same card) already is the real, existing tap-to-jump mechanism, labeled by the specific related entry rather than by category.

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean) and `npx eslint` on the one touched file (`app/(tabs)/purple-digest.tsx`, clean) -- no `lib/digest/*.ts` content files were touched this pass, so `PURPLE_DIGEST_VERSION` was deliberately left unbumped, matching how prior pure-UI Digest changes this session were handled. **Not yet exercised on-device** -- this is a real, substantial interaction change to the primary way every condition is read, genuinely more so than most "not yet exercised" items already flagged throughout this document, worth a real, careful on-device walkthrough (the persistent search bar's reveal behavior, the pillar shelves across a few different conditions, the tying-together card, cross-lens ref-collision fix) before trusting it fully.

**A real, direct follow-up correction the same day: "Search the whole digest should be on the outside of Basic Health, not inside of it. Basic Health needs its own search utility, just as all of the other areas of the Digest do," plus a real request for genuine tree-style, hierarchical navigation ("all of the deep dive into macro, micro, acid, and hormone related nutrients should be one of the topics to dive into from the hierarchical structure").**

**Global "Search All" removed as a pickable LensHub tile entirely, staying purely the persistent top-of-screen bar built earlier the same day.** Previously it sat as a co-equal grid tile right alongside Basic Health and every condition, reading as "one of the topics" rather than the structurally separate, always-available capability it was meant to be. `lens` can still resolve to `'search'` internally (typing in the persistent bar does that, reusing the same results-rendering branch unchanged), it just never appears in `LENSES` anymore. Its own dedicated Info-sheet content was folded into the screen's regular help sections instead, since there's no longer a per-lens Info tile for it to hang off of.

**Every real category, not just Basic Health, now has its own separate, scoped "search within this section" box.** `basicHealthSearchQuery` was generalized into one shared `categorySearchQuery` state, rendered for every non-search lens (Basic Health and all 18 conditions alike), independent of the global bar -- reading directly from what the request named as a real gap ("just as all of the other areas of the Digest do").

**Basic Health rebuilt from a flat, 31-group, all-shown-at-once shelf list into a real, 2-level tree** -- a direct, considered response to the person's own UX principle ("moving strictly from broad categories down to highly specific, bite-sized pieces of information") applied to the one place in the Digest that genuinely needed it (conditions, with only 4 pillars each, already read fine as a flat shelf list; Basic Health's 31 groups did not). `BASIC_HEALTH_TOPICS` replaces the old flat `BASIC_HEALTH_GROUPS`: 9 standalone topics (Glossary, Problem Foods & Swaps, Food Additives, Nutrient Interactions, Fermented Foods, Lifestyle & Environment, Mitochondria & Metabolism, Self Advocacy, Food Industry & History) plus one real parent topic, "Essential Nutrients," itself containing the 22 individual nutrient deep-dives (Magnesium through Hormones) as real subtopics -- exactly the example given directly ("all of the deep dive into macro, micro, acid, and hormone related nutrients should be one of the topics"). Top level shows a real, scannable grid of 10 topic cards; drilling into Essential Nutrients shows a second grid of 22 subtopic cards; any real leaf (standalone topic, or one specific nutrient) shows a plain, scannable list of that leaf's own entries, reusing `DigestCard` exactly as every other category's own accordion list already does. A real, dynamic "More" safety net (not a hardcoded 32nd topic) only appears if some future entry's own id genuinely matches no known prefix.

**A real, pre-existing bug was caught and fixed while validating this new tree against all 296 real Basic Health entries before shipping** (the same throwaway-script discipline already established throughout this whole Digest build) -- the OLD flat list's own "Hormones" prefix (`'hormone'`) never actually matched 11 of that topic's own 12 real entries, since `lib/digest/hormones.ts` names most of its ids after the specific hormone itself (`insulin-`, `cortisol-`, `estrogen-`, `leptin-`, `testosterone-`, `thyroid-hormones-`), not a shared `hormone-` prefix. This wasn't introduced by the restructure -- it was already silently dropping those 11 entries into the old flat list's own unlabeled "More" bucket, just harder to notice there. Fixed with the real, complete prefix list; re-validated afterward with zero unmatched entries across all 296.

Real, always-searchable independent of any tree depth confirmed to remain true: `searchDigestEntries`/`searchEntries` operate over the flat `ALL_DIGEST_ENTRIES`/category `entries` arrays regardless of the browsing UI on top of them, so every nutrient deep-dive stays fully reachable via both the persistent global bar and Basic Health's own local search exactly as before, per the request's own explicit requirement ("can also be found through either the whole digest search or through the search within each section").

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean) and `npx eslint` (clean) on the one touched file. No `lib/digest/*.ts` content files touched (840 unique ids confirmed unchanged), so `PURPLE_DIGEST_VERSION` was left unbumped. **Not yet exercised on-device** -- this is a real, further extension of the same-day interaction change to how Basic Health specifically is browsed, on top of the condition-pillar change already flagged as unverified; worth checking together in one real walkthrough once on-device access is available (search-bar placement/behavior, the topic grid, drilling into Essential Nutrients, a leaf list, and the back-navigation at each level).

**Two more real, direct corrections the same day, both fixed together: "First, move the 'Search the whole digest' search utility out of the Basic Health area and into the Digest LensHub menu as a selection. The hierarchical structure is much better, however there is no way to back out of an area to go back to the level before, all the way to the Digest home screen with the LensHub menu showing so the user can choose another lens if they want to."**

**Search All's own placement was actually wrong in the immediately preceding pass, not just re-litigated.** The persistent top-of-screen bar built earlier the same day was a real misread of "outside of Basic Health, not inside of it" -- the actual ask, now stated precisely, was for Search to be reachable as "a selection" from the same LensHub menu every other category already lives in, not a second, parallel input mechanism sitting outside that menu altogether. Reverted cleanly: the persistent bar (and its own `persistentSearchBar` style) is gone; `'search'` is a real `LensHub` tile again, leading the list (before Basic Health), with its own dedicated Info-sheet content restored (`DIGEST_SEARCH_HELP`, a real two-section write-up, not folded into the screen-level help sections the way the prior pass had left it). The `lens === 'search'` branch got its own in-content search input back, since there's no longer an always-visible bar to write into it from outside. Since `LensHub`'s own grid already renders Basic Health and every condition as plain, equal siblings, giving Search its own tile in that same list already satisfies "outside of Basic Health" on its own -- a sibling selection, not a child of Basic Health's own tree, which is what the request actually meant.

**A real, previously-unaddressed navigation gap, fixed with a new, always-present "‹ Back to Digest" link.** Before this, once any lens was picked and its content revealed, there was no way back to the tab's own true resting state (nothing picked, corner button and `PageIdentityLabel`'s own prompt showing) except tapping the corner LensHub button again -- which reopens the picker directly, not the resting screen itself. Basic Health's own tree already had a real "back one level" link (`BasicHealthTree`'s own `onBack`), but that only steps between tree levels, and stops entirely once back at Basic Health's own top-level topic grid; conditions had no back affordance of any kind. Fixed with a new, second, separate `TouchableOpacity` rendered at the very top of every revealed lens's content (above `headerCard`, inside every branch -- Search, Basic Health at any tree depth, and every condition alike), reading "‹ Back to Digest," calling `setRevealed(false)` on tap -- the exact same resting state every other tab in this app already uses, so tapping the corner button from there to pick a different lens is the same, already-familiar motion as opening this tab for the first time, not a new mechanism. Deliberately does NOT also auto-reopen the LensHub popup itself (the existing `useAutoOpenLensHubSignal` mechanism is built for cross-tab TabHub navigation specifically and already has real, documented history of bugs around swipe-vs-tap-triggered auto-opening -- reusing it here for a same-screen "back" tap risked reintroducing that same class of bug for a benefit the request didn't actually ask for). Basic Health's own existing per-level "‹ [Parent Level]" back link is untouched and still there for stepping up one tree level at a time -- the two coexist: a card deep in a Basic Health subtopic shows both "‹ Essential Nutrients" (one level up) and "‹ Back to Digest" (all the way out) at once.

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean across the whole project) and `npx eslint` (clean on the one touched file, `app/(tabs)/purple-digest.tsx`; a full-project sweep confirmed the remaining 430 `react/no-unescaped-entities` errors elsewhere are all pre-existing and untouched by this pass). No `lib/digest/*.ts` content files touched (840 unique ids, zero duplicates, zero dangling `relatedIds`, confirmed unchanged), so `PURPLE_DIGEST_VERSION` was left unbumped. **Not yet exercised on-device** -- both fixes are real, structural corrections to the exact interaction flow already flagged as unverified twice earlier the same day; worth a real, careful on-device walkthrough of all three passes together (search reachable from the LensHub grid, Basic Health's tree, and the new back-to-home link from every depth) before treating any of this session's Purple Digest layout work as settled.

**"Continue with the rest of the additional things" -- the two remaining real, contained wins from the original knowledge-base-design discussion, both built the same day: a TL;DR box, minimal inline bold-text support, and thumbs-up/down feedback.** The two larger, deliberately-deferred items from that same discussion (Pattern Reminders tied to tracked symptom/food data, and Direct-to-Tracker action buttons) remain untouched -- both need real cross-tab integration into Bio-Compass/Schedule, not a same-pass addition, and stay flagged as a separate, bigger future initiative rather than rushed in here.

**TL;DR box, built with zero new content authored.** Every entry already carries a short, one-line `teaser` (shown above every collapsed card) -- rather than invent a new field that would need populating across all 840 existing entries, the same teaser text now also renders as a real, visually distinct tinted callout (`TldrBox`, bordered, labeled "TL;DR") at the very top of the expanded detail view, above the full write-up. A small, deliberate visual duplication (the plain preview line stays above the card too, unchanged) in exchange for zero content-authoring debt.

**Minimal inline bold-text support, confirmed a genuinely safe no-op today before shipping.** `renderRichText()` splits a body of text on `**bold like this**` markers and renders the wrapped phrase with real bold weight, falling back to plain text everywhere else -- checked directly via grep across all of `lib/digest/*.ts` first and confirmed zero existing entries use this syntax anywhere, so this is pure, additive infrastructure a future entry can opt into, not a retrofit. Wired into `entry.summary` (DigestEntry) and `entry.problem`/`entry.mechanism` (ProblemFoodEntry) -- the two longest-form fields, where a bolded key phrase would actually help a reader scan.

**Thumbs-up/down feedback, deliberately local-only, no aggregation.** New `lib/digestFeedback.ts`, mirroring `lib/visualPreferences.ts`'s own already-established single-JSON-blob-under-one-`app_meta`-key pattern (simplified further here, since Purple Digest only ever has one mounted screen instance, so no cross-screen subscriber list is needed the way visual preferences requires). `FeedbackRow`, a new self-contained component rendered at the bottom of every expanded card's own detail view, loads and saves its own one entry's value directly by `entry.id` rather than being threaded as props through `BasicHealthTree`/`BasicHealthShelves` (both already several props deep) -- real thumbs-up/thumbs-down icons, tapping the already-active choice again clears it back to no opinion. This is a personal "did this land for me" mark, the same local-first spirit as the rest of this app's own health data, not a rating meant to be pooled across users -- no aggregation, no server, no analytics; a real future pass could surface "entries I've marked down" as its own filter, but that's not built here.

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean across the whole project) and `npx eslint` (clean on both touched/new files, `app/(tabs)/purple-digest.tsx` and `lib/digestFeedback.ts`; full-project sweep confirmed the same 430 pre-existing, unrelated errors, zero new ones). No `lib/digest/*.ts` content files touched. **Not yet exercised on-device** -- same standing caveat as the rest of this session's Digest layout work; the feedback mechanism specifically (a brand-new `app_meta` write path) is worth a real device check that a tap actually persists across a re-expand before trusting it fully.

**Every category's own local search box turned into a sticky subheader, the content below filtered against its real hierarchical structure rather than swapped for a flat list, same day, direct request: "move the internal search utility to the top and make it the subheader that stays at the top under the app header and all things below in the knowledgebase hierarchical set of the area are displayed below and filtered to display the specific topics of interest that are related to what they searched for," explicitly citing the earlier same-day persistent whole-Digest search bar as the precedent to match.**

**A real layout split, not just moving one element.** Every revealed lens's content used to live entirely inside one `ScrollView` -- the back link, the category header, the search box, and the actual hierarchical content all scrolled away together. That `ScrollView` is now wrapped in a real `screenColumn` flex container alongside a new, separate `fixedHeader` View sitting above it (back link, header card, and the search input, in that order) -- `fixedHeader` never scrolls; only the real content below it does, inside the unchanged `ScrollView`. A real bottom border marks where the fixed strip ends and the scrollable area begins. `lens === 'search'`'s own `searchQuery` and every other lens's shared `categorySearchQuery` now feed the exact same one input via a small `activeSearchValue`/`setActiveSearchValue` pairing, rather than two separately-rendered boxes in two different branches.

**The real, more substantial half of the request: filtering now happens against each category's own real hierarchical groups, not a flat, undifferentiated results list.** The old behavior swapped the whole tree/shelf view out for a plain list of `SearchResultCard`s the moment `categorySearchQuery` had text -- functionally a search, but not "the knowledgebase hierarchical set of the area... displayed below and filtered" the way this request asked for. Now, typing in the box keeps the SAME real grouped shape every category already shows, just filtered: a new `basicHealthAllGroups()` returns every real Basic Health leaf group at once (every standalone topic and every Essential Nutrients subtopic individually, not drilled into one at a time), and a condition's own real pillar groups (plus its closing "tying together" synthesis, folded in as one more real group) get reused directly from the already-existing `groupConditionEntries()`. Both feed through one shared filter step -- each group's own entries narrowed to just the ones matching the search, any group that ends up empty dropped outright -- straight into the existing `BasicHealthShelves` component, the same shelf-row-plus-detail-panel rendering every category already uses when NOT searching. No new rendering component was needed; the filtered view IS the normal view, just narrowed.

**A real, precise bug avoided by keeping the group's own display text and its scroll-target key as two different derived values from one shared string, not the same thing.** `shelfGroupKeyForEntry()` (already existing, used by `toggleEntry` to scroll a newly-expanded card's own group into view) computes a Basic Health entry's group key as its real `'::'`-joined tree path, and a condition's closing synthesis entry's key as the existing `TYING_TOGETHER_GROUP_KEY` constant -- both intentionally NOT pretty display strings. `basicHealthAllGroups()` and the new filtered-condition-groups step both deliberately reuse those exact same raw keys as each group's own `label`, so a shelf tap in the new filtered view scrolls to the right place with zero changes needed to `shelfGroupKeyForEntry`/`toggleEntry` themselves -- and a new `shelfGroupDisplayLabel()` helper, called only at render time inside `BasicHealthShelves`, converts that raw key into what a person actually reads (`"Essential Nutrients::Magnesium"` → `"Essential Nutrients › Magnesium"`; `TYING_TOGETHER_GROUP_KEY` → `"Putting It Together"`; a plain condition pillar label passes through unchanged, since it's neither special shape). Getting this backwards (using a pretty label as the real key) would have silently broken scroll-to-group specifically while searching, without breaking anything `tsc` or a casual read would catch.

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean across the whole project) and `npx eslint` (clean on the one touched file; a full-project sweep confirmed the same 430 pre-existing, unrelated errors, zero new ones introduced). No `lib/digest/*.ts` content files touched. **Confirmed working on-device, same day, direct feedback: "the sticky search works beautifully."** The sticky header, the filtered/grouped hierarchical search view, and the shelf-tap-scrolls-to-the-right-group mechanism are all now real, confirmed-working pieces of this app, not just reasoned-through code.

**Two more real, direct corrections the same day: the header card needed to scroll, not stay fixed, and the search boxes were reported genuinely slow to react -- both fixed together.**

**"The search utility is supposed to be above the generic about this section box and that box should scroll under it just as the rest would. Only the search utility and the breadcrumb navigation remain in the subheader."** The fixed subheader built earlier the same day had three things pinned above the ScrollView (back link, header card, search box) -- a real overreach of what was actually asked for. `headerCard` (the icon/title/description block) moved back into the ScrollView as its own first real scrolling item, exactly like every other piece of content below it; only the "‹ Back to Digest" breadcrumb and the search input itself stay in `fixedHeader` now, with the search box sitting below the breadcrumb, above where `headerCard` now scrolls past underneath it.

**"The keyboard is very slow to react, just like it was when working in the food builder lenses before that you fixed."** A real, correctly-diagnosed instance of the same class of bug already root-caused once before (see the 2026-08-02 AppKeyboard input-lag entry earlier in this document) -- but a different specific mechanism this time, not a regression in the already-fixed `AppTextInput.tsx` registration effect (confirmed still correct on inspection). The real cause here: `categorySearchQuery`/`searchQuery` are owned directly by `PurpleDigestScreen` itself, a very large component -- every keystroke forced React to re-render the WHOLE screen, and the same-day filtered-hierarchy feature (built directly above this entry) made that re-render substantially heavier than the old flat results list, recomputing `basicHealthAllGroups()`/`groupConditionEntries()` and reconciling potentially dozens of real shelf/card components synchronously on every single character, dragging down how quickly the custom on-screen keyboard could register the next tap -- the same underlying shape (a heavy owning screen blocking per-keystroke responsiveness) as the original Food-builder bug, just triggered by expensive DERIVED rendering here instead of AppKeyboard's own internal registration.

Fixed with a new, real, reusable `hooks/useDebouncedValue.ts` (no debounce hook existed anywhere in this codebase before this) -- the search box's own displayed text stays bound directly to the raw, instant `searchQuery`/`categorySearchQuery` state, so typing itself never visibly lags; the EXPENSIVE derived work (`searchResults`, and a new `categorySearchGroups`) now reads a debounced (200ms) copy of that same query instead, computed via real `useMemo` calls rather than the inline IIFEs the filtered-hierarchy feature had used. A real, related bug caught by `eslint`'s own `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` warning while wiring this in, not missed: `entries` itself was a plain, unmemoized expression (`getEntriesForCategory(lens)` returns a freshly-built array every call), which would have handed `categorySearchGroups` a new array identity on every render regardless of whether `lens` actually changed -- silently defeating the whole memo. Fixed by wrapping `entries` in its own `useMemo(() => ..., [lens])` too.

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean across the whole project) and `npx eslint` (clean on both touched/new files -- the exhaustive-deps warning above was fixed, not suppressed; a full-project sweep confirmed the same 430 pre-existing, unrelated errors, zero new ones). No `lib/digest/*.ts` content files touched. **Not yet exercised on-device** -- the debounce fix specifically is worth a real, careful on-device check (typing quickly into a category search box and confirming the keyboard itself now stays responsive, with results catching up ~200ms after typing pauses) before trusting it fully.

**Two more real, direct requests the same day: "It is looking better. Two things. When I [hit] back to digest breadcrumb from any section, it should close the current section and display the Digest LensHub menu... And, when I start to search in any section... the search results should automatically be displayed right below the subheader... without having to scroll to find them."**

**The "‹ Back to Digest" link now reopens LensHub itself, not just the resting screen.** The earlier same-day design deliberately did NOT do this ("Deliberately does NOT also auto-reopen the LensHub popup itself... risked reintroducing that same class of bug for a benefit the request didn't actually ask for") -- now directly requested, so it's built the safe way that earlier reasoning was actually worried about losing: reusing the real, narrow `autoOpenSignal` mechanism already built the same day for TabHub navigation (`useAutoOpenLensHubSignal`/`LensHub`'s own `autoOpenSignal` prop), which only ever fires from a genuine, deliberate signal, never a horizontal swipe between tabs (the exact failure mode two much earlier, reverted "always auto-open" attempts hit). A new local `openTrigger` state combines BOTH real sources -- a genuine TabHub navigation (still synced in via a `useEffect` watching `autoOpenLensHub`) and this screen's own "‹ Back to Digest" tap (bumping `openTrigger` to a fresh `` `back-${Date.now()}` `` value in the same press handler that resets `revealed`) -- so either one can independently trigger a fresh open at its own time, with LensHub's own already-existing "is this genuinely a new value" dedup deciding whether to actually show the popup. No swipe path touches `openTrigger` at all, so the original swipe-through-friction risk still can't recur through this new path either.

**Search results now appear directly under the fixed subheader, with nothing to scroll past to find them.** Two real, independent parts, matching the two options the request itself named. First, "moving the section specific starting box up out of the way": a new `isSearchActive` (the RAW, instant search value, not the debounced copy driving the actual results -- the goal here is a UI that reacts the moment typing starts, not once results catch up) hides `headerCard` outright the instant a real search begins, so results become the literal first thing inside the ScrollView rather than something sitting below a header block. Second, a real guard against a stale scroll position: a new effect watches `isSearchActive` transition from false to true and snaps the ScrollView back to the top at that exact moment -- covers the case where someone had already scrolled deep into a shelf or Basic Health's tree before starting to type, which hiding `headerCard` alone wouldn't fix (RN's ScrollView doesn't automatically reset scroll position just because the content below a given offset got shorter).

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean across the whole project) and `npx eslint` (clean on the one touched file; a full-project sweep confirmed the same 430 pre-existing, unrelated errors, zero new ones). No `lib/digest/*.ts` content files touched. **Both fixes now confirmed working on-device.** The breadcrumb-reopen half needed a real, separate root-cause fix first (`LensHub`'s own `cardReady` bug, see the later entry below) before it held up under a genuine fresh reload -- confirmed fixed the same day ("Fully closed and reopened, no more drop-in glitch"). **A real, direct regression report the same day, on-device, the first real confirmation any of this session's Purple Digest work has gotten: "It works but it introduces the LensHub menu drop in from above glitch, but it only happens when using the back to digest breadcrumb and from any of the Digest lenses."** This is the app's own long-known, previously-shelved popup-drop-in bug (see the 2026-08-01 entries earlier in this document) -- confirmed there as gated on "something else on screen doing significant animated layout work at the same moment the popup's own layout commits" (originally traced to `WheelPicker`, later removed from the app entirely, with the bug's own retest never actually happening). This report is the first real evidence of a NEW, different trigger for the same underlying class of problem, not the old one recurring -- `WheelPicker` genuinely doesn't exist anymore, so something else in the new "Back to Digest" flow specifically is now producing that same condition.

Root cause, reasoned through directly rather than guessed: the breadcrumb's own `onPress` bumped `openTrigger` (opening the popup) in the exact same synchronous tap that reset `revealed` to false -- meaning this screen's own large ScrollView (potentially dozens of real `DigestCard`/`ShelfTabCard` components, several wrapped in `Animated.View` with `LinearTransition`) was still mid-unmount at the EXACT instant LensHub's popup began its own opening animation, precisely the "two heavy visual transitions landing on the same instant" condition already established as this bug's real trigger. This never happened via the pre-existing TabHub-navigation-driven auto-open path, since arriving via a real navigation event means the destination screen's own heavy content was never mounted to begin with -- nothing to unmount at the same moment.

Fixed the same way this exact app already solves the mirror-image version of this same problem: `LensHub.tsx`'s own `choose()` function closes its popup first, THEN waits `TAB_REVEAL_DURATION_MS` (this app's one shared, real "standard transition" timing constant, not a second, separately-tuned number) before calling `onSelect` -- explicitly built so closing this popup and revealing new content never land on the same instant. `openTrigger`'s own bump now gets the same treatment in the other direction: `setRevealed(false)` fires immediately, and `setOpenTrigger(...)` is deferred behind a `setTimeout(..., TAB_REVEAL_DURATION_MS)` -- by the time it fires, the ScrollView content this tap just hid has already finished unmounting, so the popup opens against a fully settled screen, the same real condition every OTHER LensHub open (a direct corner-button tap, a genuine TabHub navigation) already enjoys.

**The delay fix above did NOT resolve it -- reported directly after a genuine, confirmed fresh reload ("Fully closed and reopened, still drops in from above") -- and this time the real, root cause was actually found, not guessed at a third time.**

**Staleness was checked and ruled out FIRST, per this project's own standing discipline, and it genuinely wasn't staleness this time -- but a real, concrete Metro problem was still found along the way, worth remembering.** The running Metro server (up since 1:42 AM) had a real, confirmed history of crash errors earlier the same session -- `ReferenceError: Property 'groupBasicHealthEntries' doesn't exist` and `ReferenceError: Property 'DIGEST_SEARCH_HELP' doesn't exist`, both real names that existed only briefly at different points during the same day's rapid iteration -- direct evidence Fast Refresh had gotten confused mid-session and could plausibly have left the phone's own JS runtime in a genuinely inconsistent state. Restarted Metro cleanly (confirmed via a real "Bundler cache is empty, rebuilding" log line, not assumed) and asked for a real, full force-stop-and-reopen -- which the person did, and the glitch still reproduced exactly the same way. This ruled staleness out as the explanation this specific time, but the Metro-crash-history discovery is real and worth remembering as its own lesson: a long-running dev server's own log is worth checking for real errors, not just assumed clean, before trusting any on-device test result either way.

**The real root cause, traced directly through `LensHub.tsx`'s own code rather than guessed**: `cardReady` (the flag gating the popup card's own visibility until Android's native Dialog window genuinely confirms it's up via `onShow` -- the app's own already-existing, hard-won fix for this exact bug class, see the 2026-08-01 entries earlier in this document) is reset to `false` by the corner button's own direct-tap `onPress` handler EVERY time, right before `setOpen(true)` -- but the `autoOpenSignal` `useEffect` (added earlier the same day for TabHub navigation, then reused for the new "Back to Digest" breadcrumb) never did that reset at all. Harmless the FIRST time a given screen's LensHub ever opens (`cardReady` already starts at its own real default, `false`) -- but every open after the first left `cardReady` sitting at whatever the PREVIOUS open had set it to (`onShow`'s own `setCardReady(true)`, never reset back when the popup closes), so a second or later auto-triggered open rendered the card at full opacity immediately, before the new Dialog window was actually confirmed up -- reproducing exactly the glitch the `onShow` gate exists to prevent. This precisely explains the reported scope ("only... from any of the Digest lenses," i.e., only once you'd already opened LensHub at least once to get there) without needing to touch timing at all.

Fixed by making the `autoOpenSignal` effect perform the exact same reset the direct corner-button tap already does -- `cardReady`, plus the scroll-hint state (`canScrollDown`/`canScrollUp`/`scrollMetrics`, a smaller instance of the identical staleness class) -- before calling `setOpen(true)`. Required reordering three hook declarations (moving `cardReady` up, and moving the whole effect itself down past `canScrollDown`/`canScrollUp`/`scrollMetrics`) so every piece of state the reset touches is already declared by the time the effect runs -- a real, valid hook reorder (all hooks still called unconditionally, every render, just in a different but still-stable order), not a conditional-hooks violation. This fix lives entirely in the shared `LensHub.tsx`, so it also closes the same latent risk for the pre-existing TabHub-navigation-driven auto-open path (`autoOpenLensHub`), not just Purple Digest's own new breadcrumb -- a real, additional benefit, not scope creep, since both paths share the exact same effect.

Metro restarted cleanly a second time after this fix specifically (`warning: Bundler cache is empty, rebuilding`, confirmed in its own log) -- a hook-declaration reorder is exactly the class of edit Fast Refresh handles least reliably, so a fresh restart was done proactively rather than risking a second false-negative retest. Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean across the whole project) and `npx eslint` (clean on the one touched file; full-project sweep confirmed the same 430 pre-existing, unrelated errors, zero new ones). **Confirmed fixed on-device the same day, after a genuine fresh full close-and-reopen: "Fully closed and reopened, no more drop-in glitch."** This closes out a real, multi-round bug -- the delay-based first attempt didn't hold up under a confirmed fresh reload, but the actual `cardReady` root cause, once correctly traced, did. Worth remembering as its own lesson alongside this document's existing Metro-staleness guidance: when a fix doesn't land, re-reading the actual mechanism from scratch (once staleness is genuinely ruled out) beats a second guess at the same kind of fix that already failed.

**The keyboard lag was real and unresolved, reported directly after the earlier debounce attempt: "The keyboard still lags."** A second, deeper investigation found the FIRST attempt's own real flaw: it debounced the EXPENSIVE derived data (`searchResults`/`categorySearchGroups`), but the raw keystroke text itself still lived in `PurpleDigestScreen`'s own state -- meaning that whole large screen (and every child it renders, including however many real shelf/card components were currently on screen) still fully re-rendered on every single character typed, REGARDLESS of the data-level memoization. Debouncing the computation never touched the actual bottleneck: React reconciling a big component tree synchronously on every keystroke, which is what was blocking the JS thread right when the custom on-screen keyboard needed to register the next tap.

**The real fix: isolate the raw keystroke into its own tiny, separate component.** New `DigestSearchInput` now owns the actual typed text as its own local state -- a cheap, isolated re-render on every character, affecting only this one small component, never `PurpleDigestScreen` itself. It only reports up to the parent via `onDebouncedChange` (the app's existing `useDebouncedValue` hook, 200ms) once typing genuinely pauses, and via a separate, INSTANT `onActiveChange` the moment its own text crosses the empty/non-empty boundary (not on every keystroke) -- letting `headerCard` hide and the results view switch on immediately without needing the parent to re-render per character to do it. `PurpleDigestScreen`'s own `searchQuery`/`categorySearchQuery` state is now, by construction, already the debounced/committed value -- the redundant second debounce layer from the first attempt was removed. A real, second bug was caught before shipping, not after: `DigestSearchInput`'s own `onChangeText` handler needed `useCallback` -- left as a plain function, its own identity would change on every keystroke-driven re-render of this SMALL component, which would have re-fired `AppTextInput`'s own registration effect and re-triggered `AppKeyboard`'s cascade on every character, silently reintroducing the exact original Food-builder-class bug at a new layer.

Reset points needed rethinking too, since the box's own value no longer lives where the reset code runs: `searchResetKey` (a new state, bumped on tab-focus loss, `jumpToRelated`, and every LensHub selection -- every place this screen already reset `searchQuery`/`categorySearchQuery` directly) is passed as `DigestSearchInput`'s own React `key`, forcing a full remount (and therefore a fresh, empty local text) whenever the box should clear -- simpler and more reliable than threading a reset signal into the child.

**A real, meaningfully smarter search followed the architecture decision above, direct request: "I want the user to search the data by questions they might have," with two real example questions ("Why do I have such a bad reaction to horchata but I can eat rice dishes without a problem?" and "What are the vitamins I need to get more of... due to my (complication here)?").** `searchEntries()`/`searchDigestEntries()` (`lib/digest/index.ts`, shared by Search All, every category's own local search, AND the same-day filtered-hierarchy feature -- one shared function, so this improves all three at once) rebuilt from a strict "every term must appear somewhere" match into a real, relevance-ranked one: a new `SEARCH_STOPWORDS` set (English question/connector words -- "why," "do," "i," "have," "can," "but," etc.) strips filler out of a typed question before matching, so a real sentence searches on its actual content words ("horchata," "reaction," "rice," "dishes") rather than requiring the exact phrase to appear verbatim anywhere (which it never would). Matching changed from AND (every term required) to OR-with-scoring (any term counts, entries ranked by how many matched, with a real title match weighted 3x an incidental body/citation mention) -- an entry genuinely about the thing being asked about now outranks one that just mentions it in passing, rather than being excluded outright for not matching every single word.

**A real bug caught by testing this against the example questions before trusting it, not after**: a bare single-letter term (a real vitamin code like "d," "a," "c," "k" -- "Vitamin D" and friends are real Digest topics) matched via plain substring is nearly useless, since ordinary English words contain almost any given letter somewhere ("and," "diet," "reaction" all contain a bare "d") -- a search for "vitamin d" was scoring nearly every entry in the whole Digest as a false "d" match, drowning out the entries genuinely about Vitamin D. Fixed with a real word-boundary check (`\bterm\b`) for any term two characters or shorter, while longer terms keep the existing, wanted substring behavior ("vitamin" matching "vitamins," "goitrogen" matching "goitrogenic," both real, already-relied-on features). Verified via a real throwaway Node script (mirroring the actual logic, not guessed) run against both example questions and a hand-built "vitamin d" ranking test before and after the word-boundary fix, confirming the false-positive was real and the fix resolved it cleanly.
