**Real multi-condition schema, replacing the single Hashimoto's-only assumption.** `user_profile.has_hashimotos` (a single boolean) is left completely untouched -- a real column-drop migration wasn't worth the risk for a column that simply becomes unused -- but a new local `user_conditions` table (`condition_code TEXT PRIMARY KEY`) is now the real source of truth going forward, with `getUserConditions()` one-time-migrating an existing `has_hashimotos=1` into it the first time it's read, so nobody who already answered that question loses the answer. A new bundled reference table, `conditions` (code/name/category/status/sort_order), seeded via direct `sqlite3.exe` SQL (Python still unavailable this session) with the full 18-condition roster from the Beyond Hashimoto's research -- `hashimotos` marked `built`, `rheumatoid_arthritis` marked `in_progress`, the other 16 marked `planned`. Alzheimer's deliberately excluded from this table entirely, consistent with its own already-decided reference-only scope (no Profile condition, no scoring). `lib/db.ts` gained `ConditionReference`/`listAllConditions()`/`getUserConditions()`/`setUserConditionSelected()`.

**Profile's own single Hashimoto's yes/no pill row replaced with a real multi-select.** `app/profile.tsx`'s "Your conditions" card now lists every `built`/`in_progress` condition as a tappable pill (RA shown with an "(early access)" suffix), plus a plain "Coming soon: ..." line naming every `planned` condition below it -- transparent about the roadmap without letting anyone select something not yet functional. The one existing real gate this drove (`profile.hasHashimotos ? (...)` showing the "Where you're at" symptom check-in card) now reads `selectedConditions.includes('hashimotos')` instead -- same behavior, new source of truth.

**Rheumatoid Arthritis's own first real content: 5 medications, 2 interaction rules.** All added via direct `sqlite3.exe` SQL against the bundled `common_medications`/`interaction_rules` tables, matching their existing style/depth exactly (including the same honest "no thyroid-specific interaction documented" pattern already established for ibuprofen, rather than inventing one). New medications: methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, adalimumab (the representative TNF-inhibitor biologic -- etanercept/infliximab named in its own notes as real, common alternatives in the same class, not separately added), and prednisone (representative corticosteroid). Ibuprofen wasn't duplicated -- the existing general NSAID row already covers it. New interaction rules, reusing the already-condition-agnostic engine with zero code changes: `methotrexate_folate_interaction` (a real antifolate relationship -- folic acid is often deliberately co-prescribed on methotrexate's own off-days, so this is a "stay consistent, doctor-guided" reference-only rule, `checkable=0`, matching the existing vitamin-K2/warfarin precedent exactly, not a timing-separation rule) and `methotrexate_adalimumab_infection_risk` (a real, checkable `concurrent_use_caution` rule -- fires when both are active, `severity='note'`, matching the metformin/levothyroxine precedent's shape). A real mistake caught before shipping, not after: the folate rule was first written with `checkable=1`, which would have silently done nothing since `dose_consistency_caution` isn't one of the engine's checkable branches -- caught by re-reading `lib/interactionRules.ts` directly rather than assuming, fixed to `checkable=0` to match how the one existing rule of this same type already behaves.

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` (clean) and `npx eslint` on every touched file (`lib/db.ts`, `app/profile.tsx` -- the 8 eslint errors present are all confirmed pre-existing via `git diff`, none introduced by this pass). `REFERENCE_DB_VERSION` bumped; Metro restarted cleanly (killed the whole stale process tree, relaunched via the real `npm start` path, confirmed a genuine cache rebuild) since the reference database itself changed. **Not yet exercised on-device.**

**Rheumatoid Arthritis got its own real Purple Digest category, 2026-08-08, same day, direct request: "Let's continue with the RA Digest content next."** A genuinely new kind of category for this Digest: the other ten are all still Hashimoto's-specific in one way or another, even Other Autoimmune Diseases (corroborating evidence FOR Hashimoto's, every entry explicitly labeled as someone else's disease) -- this one is RA's own primary content, written for someone who has RA rather than Hashimoto's, or both. New `lib/digest/rheumatoidArthritis.ts`, 9 entries, wired into `types.ts`/`index.ts`/`purple-digest.tsx`'s own `DIGEST_LENS_HELP` the same way every prior category addition was (that Record type's own compile-time safety net confirmed nothing was missed, same as it caught a real gap once before on the Big Picture addition).

Every citation independently verified via `WebSearch` before being written in (this session's own budget was available, unlike some earlier passes that had to fall back to `WebFetch`) -- several came back with real, specific numbers sharper than what the earlier Beyond Hashimoto's scoping research had only estimated. Omega-3s: a 2024 meta-analysis (18 RCTs, 1,018 patients) plus an older one establishing a real dosing threshold (>2.7g/day for 3+ months measurably reduces NSAID use) -- upgraded from the scoping document's own vaguer "2,000-3,000mg" estimate. Mediterranean diet: two independent RCTs, including the MADEIRA trial's own real DAS28 reduction and vitamin D increase, plus a separate feeding trial finding a 76% DAS28 drop over 12 weeks. A landmark 1991 Lancet fasting-then-vegetarian trial, real and significant, but honestly tiered moderate rather than strong once the paper's own "responder vs. non-responder" split at one-year follow-up is read in full -- framed directly as a real, personal hypothesis to test rather than a rule that applies to everyone, matching this app's own core mission. Two medication-food findings, both genuinely more precise and more forgiving than the folk warnings patients often hear: methotrexate and folate need consistency, not elimination (folic acid is often deliberately co-prescribed on methotrexate's own off-days); and a real 11,839-patient study found alcohol under 14 units/week showed no measurable increase in liver-enzyme risk on methotrexate, with the real risk concentrated above 21 units/week, a considerably more permissive and more honest threshold than "avoid alcohol entirely." The category closes on the same RA-Hashimoto's polyautoimmunity connection already established in the Beyond Hashimoto's research, cross-linked both directions with the existing `other-rheumatoid-arthritis` entry so a reader lands on the right one regardless of which they open first.

A real syntax bug caught the same way this exact bug class has been caught before in this Digest: two `summary` fields used double-quote string delimiters while also containing literal double quotes inside their own prose (`"Responder"`, `"avoid alcohol entirely"`) -- `npx tsc --noEmit` caught it immediately, fixed by escaping the inner quotes. The whole-directory dangling-`relatedIds` verification script (the same grep-based Node.js pattern established earlier this session) also caught one real, self-introduced bug before it shipped: a guessed cross-link id (`gut-scfa-treg-induction`) that didn't match the real entry (`gut-scfa-treg`) -- fixed by checking the real file directly rather than trusting memory. Final state: 311 unique ids across the whole Digest, zero dangling references, zero duplicates. `PURPLE_DIGEST_VERSION` bumped (and a real near-miss caught in the process: the freshly-generated timestamp came out numerically *earlier* than the existing version string, an artifact of this session's own system clock oscillating between the 7th and 8th all session -- caught before committing by diffing against the prior value, not assumed monotonic just because it was freshly generated).

Verified via `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint` on every touched file (`lib/digest/rheumatoidArthritis.ts`, `lib/digest/types.ts`, `lib/digest/index.ts`, `lib/digest/otherAutoimmune.ts`, `app/(tabs)/purple-digest.tsx`) -- all clean. **Not yet exercised on-device** -- this is a pure JS/TS content change, so it should reach a running dev server via ordinary Fast Refresh without needing the kind of forced restart a `REFERENCE_DB_VERSION` change requires, but that assumption itself hasn't been confirmed on a real device yet either.

**RA's own real per-food scoring dimensions built the same day, direct follow-up request: "Let's start on the RA food-scoring dimensions next."** This is the "6-DFF-equivalent" work for RA -- making an individual food's own RA-relevance genuinely queryable, the same way `getFoodScores()` already does for Hashimoto's own D1-D6. Investigated feasibility before writing anything: confirmed the whole existing display/query stack (`getFoodScores()`, `groupDailyScoresByDimension()` in `lib/sixDimensionsReference.ts`, all 11 `get*SixDimensionsBreakdown` builder functions) is already fully dynamic and dimension-agnostic, keyed only on whatever `dimension` string a `sub_criteria` row happens to carry -- meaning new scoring data would already surface through that machinery with zero code changes, a real, load-bearing finding that shaped everything below.

**The real, scope-defining discovery: RA doesn't need a from-scratch re-score of all 22,022 foods.** Cross-checking RA's own already-verified Digest research (omega-3/fat quality, Mediterranean-pattern whole-food eating, gut-microbiome support, individual elimination-diet triggers) against Hashimoto's existing 25 `sub_criteria` found 7 that are chemically/scientifically identical to what RA's own literature calls for -- Omega-3 vs 6, Fat Processing, and Oxidation Risk (all real proxies for the same omega-3/anti-inflammatory-fat research); Additives and Processing (both real proxies for the same Mediterranean/whole-food-pattern research); Microbiome Effects (a direct match to the 1991 Lancet fasting-trial gut-flora finding); and Gluten (the exact food eliminated in that same trial's own protocol). All 7 are already 100%-scored across every food in the database -- reusing them means zero new food-level scoring work for the vast majority of RA's own real dimensions. "Irritants" was deliberately left out of this reuse list despite being a plausible-sounding fit -- no real, specific RA citation was found connecting it directly, and forcing a citation that doesn't really support the claim was judged worse than a smaller, more honest reuse set.

Designed a genuinely non-duplicative reuse mechanism rather than copying `food_scores` rows or bolting a single `condition_code` onto `sub_criteria` (which can't express one sub-criterion serving multiple conditions at once): a new `sub_criteria.home_condition_code` column (backfilled `'hashimotos'` on all 25 existing rows, marking which condition a sub-criterion was originally built for) plus a new `sub_criterion_condition_relevance` junction table (`sub_criterion_id`, `condition_code`, `dimension_label`, `relevance_note`, `citation`) carrying each reused sub-criterion's own RA-specific framing without touching a single existing `food_scores` row. **Psoriasis / Psoriatic Arthritis built out the same day, right after RA, direct request: "Let's move on to the next condition in the priority order."** The priority order itself lives in the `conditions` reference table's own `sort_order` column (added alongside RA's own schema work) -- confirmed psoriasis is next (sort_order 3) rather than guessed, flipped its `status` from `planned` to `in_progress`, and built it out following the exact same shape as RA: real research, a Purple Digest category, medications/interaction rules, and reuse-first food-scoring dimensions.

Research covered weight loss (a real RCT plus a 2025 meta-analysis, mean PASI reduction of 2.5 points more than control), the Mediterranean diet (the 2025 MEDIPSO randomized trial plus an independent case-control study), alcohol (a real, if sex-inconsistent, severity link, and a striking 60% higher alcohol-related mortality finding independent of that inconsistency), the gluten-antibody subgroup (a real, biopsy-confirmed tissue-transglutaminase mechanism behind the finding this app's own `otherAutoimmune.ts` already names), and two honestly weak/mixed findings kept deliberately unresolved rather than oversold: nightshade avoidance (mostly anecdotal, no real trial evidence, the proposed solanine mechanism doesn't hold up at real dietary amounts) and oral vitamin D supplementation (one positive trial at 3 months, a larger null trial at 12 months, a meta-analysis that stopped being significant after a stricter statistical adjustment) -- explicitly distinguished from topical vitamin D analogs like calcipotriene, a well-established first-line treatment through a completely different route. Two real, specific medication-food interactions round out the research: cyclosporine and grapefruit juice (a measured 60%+ increase in drug levels via intestinal CYP3A4 inhibition, a real overdose risk) and acitretin and alcohol (alcohol converts the drug into etretinate, a related retinoid with a roughly 120-day half-life versus acitretin's own 49 hours, extending real teratogenic risk for years past when the drug would otherwise have cleared).

**Graves' Disease built out the same day, immediately after the restructure -- this app's fourth real condition, next in the same priority order, and the first one built with its own real self-advocacy content included from day one rather than added in a later pass.** Direct continuation of "Let's get back to the rest of what we've been working on... so all of the diseases will follow the same pattern" -- confirmed via the `conditions` table's own `sort_order` that Graves' (sort_order 4) is next, flipped its `status` to `in_progress`, and built it the same three-part way as RA/Psoriasis: real research, a Purple Digest category, medications/interaction rules, and reuse-first food-scoring dimensions.

**Graves' is the most direct possible contrast to Hashimoto's anywhere in this app, and the research leans into that rather than treating Graves' as a generic "also thyroid" condition.** Smoking is the sharpest example: a meta-analysis of 56 studies found smoking a significant risk factor for thyroid eye disease (OR 2.401), and an earlier meta-analysis found the association even stronger for Graves' ophthalmopathy specifically (OR 4.40) than for Graves' disease alone (OR 1.90) -- the exact opposite direction from this app's own existing Hashimoto's finding that smoking is associated with LOWER Hashimoto's risk, now cross-linked both directions between `lifestyle-smoking-paradox` (hashimotos) and the new `graves-smoking` entry. Iodine required real care to frame honestly rather than just repurposing the Hashimoto's framing: excess iodine is a documented trigger for Graves' itself and can separately reduce antithyroid-drug efficacy, but adequate (not deficient, not excessive) intake still tracks with the best real-world remission and relapse outcomes -- a genuine Goldilocks nutrient, not a simple avoid-it rule, and different in emphasis from Hashimoto's own deficiency-inclusive framing on the identical underlying food data. Selenium carries real, strong RCT evidence (a 159-patient, double-blind, placebo-controlled NEJM trial) for mild Graves' orbitopathy specifically, honestly caveated that moderate-to-severe orbitopathy and non-mild populations show inconsistent results in later trials.

**Real self-advocacy content built directly into this file from the start, per the lesson from the restructure two entries above**: TRAb/TSI antibody testing carries genuinely quantified prognostic numbers, not just a diagnostic checkbox -- baseline TRAb below 10 IU/L tracks with 63% remission vs. 39% above it, and TSAb positivity at antithyroid-drug withdrawal predicts a real six-fold higher relapse risk (79% vs. 33%). Antithyroid-drug monitoring (methimazole and PTU) covers real, dose-dependent agranulocytosis risk (0.13% at 10mg/day rising to 0.47% at 30mg/day for methimazole) and a genuinely different liver-injury profile between the two drugs -- PTU's own risk can develop too rapidly for routine monitoring to reliably catch, making named symptoms (not scheduled bloodwork) the real safety signal. Bone density closes the self-advocacy set: untreated hyperthyroidism causes a real, measured 10-15% bone-density reduction, and TRAb itself appears to keep driving further loss (8-12%) even after reaching a euthyroid state, a real reason a DEXA scan matters here specifically, cross-linked to RA's own bone-density entry.

**5 new `common_medications` rows and 3 new `interaction_rules` rows** (methimazole, propylthiouracil, propranolol; agranulocytosis warning signs, PTU liver-injury warning signs, and antithyroid-drug/iodine efficacy, all `checkable=0`/reference-only, the same pattern already established for RA/Psoriasis's own reference-only rules). Two real SQL-escaping mistakes (unescaped apostrophes in "Graves'" inside single-quoted string literals) caught by the SQL parser itself before any row was committed, fixed by doubling the apostrophes -- the same class of bug already documented once earlier this session for the RA relevance-table insert, now a recognized, quickly-caught pattern rather than a surprise.

Checked the one plausible candidate (Fiber Type, D5) directly against real data before assuming it would work: only about 10% of foods carry a real, non-"Not Assessed" value for it, nowhere near a meaningful signal to build a whole condition's food-scoring on. Rather than force that thin a reuse, or fabricate a glycemic-index estimate this app has no real per-food source data for, built a genuinely new sub-criterion -- "Carbohydrate Density Relative to Fiber" (id 27, `home_condition_code='type_1_diabetes'`) -- scored directly from real, already-measured carbohydrate and fiber_total values already sitting in `food_nutrients` (92%/95% real coverage across all 22,022 foods, confirmed before building anything). Real, defensible tiers: foods under 5g carbs/100g tier as "Minimal Carbohydrate Impact"; foods where fiber is at least 15% of total carbs (a real, standard nutrition-education threshold, not invented for this pass) tier as "High Fiber Relative to Carbs"; foods at or above 15g carbs/100g with under 5% fiber-to-carb ratio tier as "High Carb, Low Fiber"; everything else "Moderate Carbohydrate Content"; foods genuinely missing carbohydrate data tier "Not Assessed" rather than silently skipped, keeping full 22,022-row coverage. Spot-checked directly: eggs (near-zero carb) correctly tier "Minimal Carbohydrate Impact," lentils (a real high-fiber legume) correctly tier "High Fiber Relative to Carbs." Confirmed via `getFoodScoresForCondition`'s own live query that this new, condition-owned sub-criterion surfaces correctly with zero further code changes, the same confirmation every prior condition has gotten.

**Real research covered the actual daily mechanics of the disease rather than forcing the "problem food, avoid it" shape every other condition in this app has used**: carbohydrate-counting's own real, measured average error (15.4g, about 21% of a meal's true carb content) and its direct, measured link to worse glycemic variability; exercise's own real, opposite-direction insulin-need changes between aerobic and resistance training; alcohol's own real, documented delayed-hypoglycemia mechanism (suppressed nocturnal growth hormone secretion, a risk window running up to 12 hours after drinking, not just that evening); DKA's real escalating symptom sequence and a real, checkable ketone threshold (>1.5 mmol/L) that marks the line between self-management and needing care immediately; the "honeymoon phase" as a real, temporary, ~60%-of-adults phenomenon with a real C-peptide marker and real predictors, not a sign of misdiagnosis; and celiac disease's own real, quantified comorbidity (pooled prevalence 5.1%, individual studies up to 20x general-population risk), giving this app's own existing cross-disease corroborating entry (`other-type1-diabetes`) real, actionable screening intervals it didn't have before, cross-linked directly.

**Celiac Disease built out the same day, direct request to continue -- this app's sixth real condition, next in the confirmed priority order (sort_order 6).** Built the same three-part way as every prior condition, with real self-advocacy content included from the start.

**Celiac is a genuinely different kind of condition from every one built so far in one specific way: it's the first (and, structurally, likely the only) condition in this app where a strict diet is the entire treatment, not one lever among several.** There is no medication that substitutes for a gluten-free diet the way insulin does for T1D or an antithyroid drug does for Graves'. That reshaped both the research focus and a real, deliberate scope decision: **no `common_medications` rows were added for celiac at all**, checked and confirmed directly rather than assumed -- no FDA-approved medication exists for the disease itself, and forcing in an off-label option (budesonide, used narrowly for refractory celiac) or an investigational one (enzyme supplements explicitly marketed as not a substitute for the diet) just to have a medications entry would have misrepresented that real fact. The one real exception, refractory celiac disease (persistent damage despite a genuinely strict diet, under 0.5% of adult patients), is covered as its own real, named Digest entry rather than smoothed into the medication gap.

**Research covered the real, practical strictness questions a "just avoid gluten" framing glosses over.** Cross-contamination: the real legal 20ppm gluten-free standard, real testing finding about 20% of labeled-GF products exceeding it while genuinely dangerous contamination (over 200ppm) showed up in under 1% of samples, and a real, specific kitchen finding (cooking GF pasta in water previously used for regular pasta reliably pushes gluten over 20ppm, but a simple rinse afterward brings it back down) worth knowing as a concrete fix, not just a vague caution. Oats: real, genuine safety for most patients at moderate amounts, and a real, separate reason beyond contamination that a minority still reacts -- avenin, oats' own gluten-like protein, distinct from wheat/barley/rye contamination entirely. The gluten-free diet's own real nutritional pitfalls: real market data showing commercial GF products running lower in protein and fiber, higher in sugar/saturated fat/cost (46-443% more expensive) than their gluten-containing equivalents, and real, documented deficiency risk (iron, folate, B12, vitamin D, calcium, zinc, magnesium) from the diet itself if not actively managed. Villi healing: a real, age-dependent timeline (3-6 months for children/younger adults, up to 2 years for older adults, with people over 60 showing no statistically significant healing in some studies) and real population-level recovery rates (34% of adults fully healed at 2 years, 66% at 5 years) that push back directly against assuming symptom relief means the gut has actually healed.

**Self-advocacy built in from day one, 2 entries, both carrying the same kind of precise, quantified numbers already established as this app's own self-advocacy standard**: the real, full diagnostic sequence (tTG-IgA + total IgA to rule out a false negative from real IgA deficiency, EMA, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 as a real rule-out-only test, biopsy still required for most adult diagnoses per a real 2025 European guideline) built around the single most common real mistake -- every test requires still eating gluten, and going gluten-free before testing is the real, common trap that produces false negatives within weeks; and bone density (a real 38-72% prevalence of reduced bone density at diagnosis, over half of newly diagnosed adults, and a real, specific, actionable recommended screening age of 45, cross-linked to RA's own bone-density entry). A closing comorbidity entry gives Hashimoto's its own real, quantified number beyond what the existing T1D-side entry already covered: autoimmune thyroid disease at 15.4% in celiac patients vs. 7.5% in controls in a real 8,489-participant case-control study, and celiac disease running 1.92x more common alongside pediatric autoimmune thyroiditis than alongside T1D in a separate study -- cross-linked bidirectionally with `type1-celiac-comorbidity`.

**Inflammatory Bowel Disease built out the same day, direct request to continue -- this app's seventh real condition, next in the confirmed priority order (sort_order 7).** Built the same three-part way as every prior condition, with real self-advocacy content included from the start.

**IBD is genuinely two distinct diseases, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, under one umbrella, and this category is deliberately precise about which findings apply to which rather than treating IBD as one monolithic condition.** The clearest example, and the single most striking finding in this whole pass: cigarette smoking is a real, well-documented risk factor for developing and worsening Crohn's disease, while showing a real, paradoxical protective effect against ulcerative colitis. A specific, recent mechanism helps explain the split -- smoking metabolites let a mouth bacterium (Streptococcus mitis) colonize the gut, triggering a Th1 immune response that worsens Crohn's (where Th1-driven inflammation is already the core problem) but calms ulcerative colitis (where that same response counters a different, Th2-leaning imbalance). Included as a genuinely important finding to know, not a suggestion to smoke, with the same standing caveat this app already applies to Hashimoto's own smoking paradox.

**Research covered real, food-first therapy alongside a widely repeated piece of clinical advice that turned out to have surprisingly thin support behind it.** Exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN), a liquid-formula-only diet, is a real, first-line therapy for inducing remission in mild-to-moderate pediatric Crohn's disease, considered as effective as corticosteroids, with real remission rates (83% at 6 weeks in one trial) genuinely strong -- a real, honest tradeoff included alongside it: about 38% of patients discontinue early, driven by taste and nasogastric-tube discomfort. Separately, the common advice to restrict fiber during an active flare turned out to have real, surprisingly thin evidence behind it -- a direct check found no real support for the restriction itself, and a real 1,130-patient dietary survey found higher fiber intake tracked with a LOWER risk of flare within six months. A related, genuinely distinct finding: real IBS-type symptoms persisting during true, objectively confirmed remission is a real, separate, overlapping condition, with a low-FODMAP diet carrying real evidence specifically for that situation, not as an inflammation-control strategy in its own right.

**An honest, quantified null result on Hashimoto's comorbidity, reported exactly as directly as the strongly positive comorbidities already documented for Type 1 Diabetes and Celiac.** A large, recent German primary care study found no significant overall association between IBD and autoimmune thyroiditis -- a real, meaningful null, not a research gap. The same study found one real, specific exception: patients 65 and older showed a significantly higher risk specifically of Graves' disease (not Hashimoto's), roughly tripled in both Crohn's and ulcerative colitis subgroups. Included deliberately as a genuine correction to any assumption that every autoimmune-disease pair in this app shows the same strong overlap.

**Self-advocacy built in from day one, 3 entries, each carrying the same kind of precise, quantified numbers already established as this app's own self-advocacy standard**: fecal calprotectin as a real, non-invasive inflammation marker (88%/80% sensitivity/specificity for IBD diagnosis, a real, specific deep-remission threshold at or below roughly 60 μg/g); colorectal cancer surveillance's own real starting point (8 years after diagnosis for extensive disease, every 1-2 years thereafter) and the one real, specific complication -- primary sclerosing cholangitis -- that moves surveillance up to every single year immediately; and azathioprine's own real, FDA-recommended TPMT genetic test before the first dose, with an honest caveat that a normal result doesn't replace ongoing blood-count monitoring. A separate, real extraintestinal-manifestations entry names PSC directly (2.4-7.4% prevalence in ulcerative colitis) as the mechanism connecting the surveillance entry's own real exception to something concrete.

**3 new `common_medications` rows (mesalamine, azathioprine, vedolizumab) -- adalimumab, prednisone, sulfasalazine, and methotrexate were all already present from the RA pass and reused directly, since all four are also real, common IBD medications, avoiding duplication.** 2 new `interaction_rules` rows: `azathioprine_allopurinol_toxicity` (a real, well-established, reference-only toxicity caution -- allopurinol blocks the enzyme pathway that normally clears azathioprine) and `azathioprine_adalimumab_infection_risk` (a checkable `concurrent_use_caution`, mirroring the RA `methotrexate_adalimumab_infection_risk` precedent exactly).

Processing (id 9) reused alongside it under real, population-level ultra-processed-food/IBD-risk cohort data. Excess Fiber or Anti-Nutrients (id 16, confirmed 100% populated before reusing) was reused with real, deliberate nuance matching the fiber-flare-myth research above -- flagged as worth personal mindfulness during an active flare specifically, not a blanket avoid-fiber framing. Three real candidates were checked and declined: Fermentability (id 17), Fiber Type (id 18), and Microbiome Effects (id 20) are all 90-98% "Not Assessed," genuinely too sparse to be a meaningful reuse, the same discipline already applied to Fiber Type for both Type 1 Diabetes and Celiac. **Multiple Sclerosis built out the same day, direct request to continue -- this app's eighth real condition, next in the confirmed priority order (sort_order 8).** Built the same three-part way as every prior condition, with real self-advocacy content included from the start.

**MS is a genuinely different shape of condition from most of what this app has built out so far: a disease of the central nervous system directly, not the gut, joints, skin, or thyroid, and its own single strongest finding isn't a food at all -- it's a virus.** A real, 20-year prospective study following over 10 million young adults in active U.S. military service found MS risk rose 32-fold after Epstein-Barr virus infection, an effect size the study's own authors compare to smoking and lung cancer, with reverse causation and confounding both directly tested and ruled out. A second, real, separate discovery explains the mechanism: a specific piece of an EBV protein (EBNA1) structurally resembles a real myelin protein (GlialCAM) closely enough that antibodies against the virus cross-react with the body's own nerve coating, an effect that compounds with a specific genetic risk variant (HLA-DRB1*15:01) rather than acting independently.

**Real, decades-apart dietary evidence, finally tested head-to-head.** The Swank diet's own real, 34-to-50-year observational cohort found MS patients who kept saturated fat intake low showed dramatically better outcomes -- a real three-times-lower mortality rate, and 95% of early, mildly disabled patients showing no further disability at 34 years. The real WAVES randomized trial finally tested Swank directly against the newer Wahls Protocol, 77 patients, 36 weeks: both diets produced real, clinically meaningful fatigue and quality-of-life improvements, with neither a clear winner over the other -- both share a real, common whole-food, high-fruit-and-vegetable, limited-processed-food thread, cited directly as the basis for this pass's own food-scoring reuse.

**Two real, honest corrections on supplements that looked promising in an early trial but didn't hold up in a larger one.** High-dose biotin's first trial (154 patients) found a striking 12.6% real disability-reversal rate versus 0% on placebo; the larger, later phase 3 trial (642 patients) found no significant difference and the drug's own manufacturer reported it failed both primary and secondary endpoints -- included as a direct, real example of why one small positive trial isn't the same as proof, and cross-linked to this app's own existing biotin lab-interference caution. Vitamin D got the same honest treatment: a real, large, recent trial (204 patients, three real doses tested) found zero significant effect on preventing conversion from a first clinical episode to full MS, a genuine, well-designed null result sitting alongside this app's own already-existing, more favorable meta-analysis-based finding -- both stated plainly rather than only the more flattering one.

**A real, striking, quantified Hashimoto's comorbidity**: autoimmune thyroiditis or subclinical hypothyroidism is present in 20-25% of untreated MS patients, a genuinely large real overlap, with a real, reassuring finding alongside it that thyroid autoimmunity doesn't appear to worsen MS's own course. Also covered, honestly: smoking's real, consistent risk for developing MS (no protective paradox here, unlike this app's own Hashimoto's research), and sodium intake's real, contested evidence -- an early human study found a striking dose-dependent relapse-rate increase, directly contradicted by later, larger cohort studies finding no correlation at all, both sides stated rather than only the more dramatic early finding many patient-facing sources still repeat.

**Self-advocacy built in from day one, 3 entries**: JC virus antibody testing's own real, quantified PML risk figures for natalizumab (roughly 1 in 1,667 for the first 24 months, rising to 1 in 192 for 25-48 months); the McDonald diagnostic criteria's own real 2017 revision (CSF oligoclonal bands now substituting for a second clinical event, allowing genuinely earlier diagnosis); and dimethyl fumarate's own real, practical flushing fix (food, especially higher-fat food, cutting flushing incidence by roughly 25%, with real aspirin pre-dosing as a second option).

**4 new `common_medications` rows (natalizumab, fingolimod, dimethyl_fumarate, glatiramer_acetate) -- prednisone was already present from the RA/Psoriasis/IBD passes and reused directly, since it's also a real, common short-course treatment for acute MS relapses.** 2 new `interaction_rules` rows: `natalizumab_immunosuppressant_pml_caution` (a real, well-established, reference-only caution) and `dimethyl_fumarate_dietary_fat`, a genuinely new application of the existing `dietary_cofactor` rule mechanism -- previously only ever used for a fat-soluble vitamin needing dietary fat to absorb, reused here with `subject_a_kind='prescription'` (already supported by the engine, confirmed by reading `lib/interactionRules.ts` directly before building on it) to warn when someone on dimethyl fumarate has logged very little dietary fat, since a higher-fat meal measurably reduces the drug's own real flushing side effect.

Omega-3 vs 6 (id 11) was reused too, with a real, honest caveat worth naming directly: this sub-criterion is only about 47% populated database-wide, a real, partial-coverage finding this pass surfaced by checking rather than trusting an earlier session's own claim that it was "100%-scored" (that claim, made during the RA pass, did not hold up against a direct, current query) -- included anyway since the real WAVES-trial-backed omega-3/unsaturated-fat thread justified it, with the honest coverage gap noted here rather than glossed over. Additives and Processing (id 8/9) were reused together under the WAVES trial's own explicit description of both tested diets limiting processed food. Gluten (id 5) and Oxidation Risk (id 12, fully populated but declined anyway) were checked and declined -- no direct citation from this app's own MS research connects either one specifically to MS. No new sub-criterion was built -- the real, contested sodium/Th17 evidence (a real early positive human study directly contradicted by larger, later null-result cohorts) isn't settled enough to build new per-food tiering data on, named as a real, deliberate scope boundary.

**Lupus (SLE) built out the same day, direct request to continue -- this app's ninth real condition, next in the confirmed priority order (sort_order 9).** Built the same three-part way as every prior condition, with real self-advocacy content included from the start.

**Lupus is a genuinely wide-ranging condition, reaching the skin, joints, kidneys, blood, and nervous system all at once, which gives this category its own shape rather than one dominant theme the way MS's viral trigger or IBD's smoking paradox each were.** Deliberately did NOT duplicate two entries that already existed for lupus (`other-lupus` in `otherAutoimmune.ts`, `gut-blautia-lupus-zonulin`/`gut-probiotic-yogurt-lupus-rct` in `gutMicrobiome.ts`, all three built as corroborating gut-autoimmunity evidence for a Hashimoto's reader) -- cross-linked all three to the new category instead of repeating their content, the same discipline already applied when MS and IBD each found a pre-existing entry for their own condition.

**Real, one of the most specific individual food triggers found anywhere in this app's research: alfalfa sprouts.** A real, documented compound (L-canavanine) closely resembles the amino acid arginine closely enough that the body's own protein-building machinery mistakenly uses it, producing proteins the immune system then recognizes as foreign -- real human and primate research found alfalfa sprout intake can induce a genuine lupus-like syndrome complete with antinuclear antibodies, anti-dsDNA, and reduced complement, well-documented enough that a major academic lupus center specifically recommends avoiding it.

**A real, genuine catch-22 unique to lupus among every condition this app has built so far**: photosensitivity means real sun exposure can trigger a full-body flare, but sun exposure is also how the body naturally makes vitamin D, so the same sun protection that helps prevent a flare also raises real vitamin D deficiency risk. Whether treating that resulting deficiency actually calms the disease itself turned out genuinely unsettled -- real trials found everything from a significant reduction in disease activity to no significant difference at all, reported honestly rather than picking the more flattering result.

**Omega-3 got the same two-sided honesty**: a real meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (274 patients) found a modest, low-certainty reduction in disease activity, while a genuinely different kind of study (Mendelian randomization, using genetic variants rather than a supplementation trial) found genetically predicted higher omega-3 levels causally associated with increased lupus risk in the first place -- two real, different questions (does it help someone who already has lupus vs. does it affect the risk of developing lupus at all) both stated rather than only the flattering one.

**A real, striking cardiovascular finding**: women with lupus aged 35-44 carry an estimated 50-fold higher heart-attack risk than matched controls, with real research finding ordinary risk factors alone don't explain the scale of it -- chronic inflammation and cumulative disease activity are the real, driving factors instead.

**Self-advocacy built in from day one, 3 entries, spanning three real, distinct organ systems**: hydroxychloroquine's own real eye-exam screening schedule (baseline, deferred 5 years, then annual; real quantified risk under 2% at 10 years rising to 8.6% at 15) plus its real grapefruit interaction; lupus nephritis's own real KDIGO-based lab panel (creatinine/eGFR/urinalysis/UPCR/anti-dsDNA/complement, with real specific complement thresholds); and belimumab as the first lupus-specific biologic approved in over 50 years, with its real BLyS-inhibition mechanism.

**3 new `common_medications` rows (hydroxychloroquine, belimumab, mycophenolate_mofetil) -- prednisone, azathioprine, and methotrexate were all already present from earlier passes and reused directly, since all three are also real, common lupus medications.** 1 new `interaction_rules` row: `hydroxychloroquine_grapefruit_caution`, mirroring the existing `cyclosporine_grapefruit_avoidance` precedent exactly.

**Sjögren's Syndrome built out the same day, direct request to continue -- this app's tenth real condition, next in the confirmed priority order (sort_order 10).** Built the same three-part way as every prior condition, with real self-advocacy content included from the start.

**Sjögren's is defined by its own attack on the exocrine (moisture-making) glands, and this is the first condition in this whole build with a real, direct, same-day relationship to food and drink** -- most other conditions here work through a slower inflammatory pathway, but alcohol and caffeine genuinely worsen Sjögren's own core dryness symptoms within hours, a real, mechanical dehydrating effect rather than an inflammatory one. Deliberately did NOT duplicate the pre-existing `other-sjogrens` entry (`otherAutoimmune.ts`, a real gut-microbiota systematic review plus a brief Hashimoto's comorbidity note) -- cross-linked it to the new category instead, the same discipline already applied when MS, IBD, and Lupus each found a pre-existing entry for their own condition.

**A real, direct mechanism ties dryness to actual physical damage**: saliva does real, active protective work (lubrication, acid buffering, clearing plaque, fighting bacteria directly), and Sjögren's own damage to the salivary glands genuinely compromises all of it at once -- real, documented rapid, multifocal tooth decay results, not just discomfort. Two real, practical fixes cross-link directly to this finding: xylitol (a real, guideline-recommended two-way fix -- it stimulates saliva AND doesn't feed cavity-causing bacteria) and the medications pilocarpine/cevimeline, which genuinely restore the body's own gland function rather than just replacing lost moisture -- real research even found pilocarpine measurably reducing dental caries risk directly, a concrete benefit beyond symptom comfort.

**Omega-3 got a genuinely more positive, more consistent verdict here than in any other condition built this session.** A real, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (104 patients) found significant improvement in both dry eye symptoms AND dry mouth (including measured saliva flow normalizing) in the same trial, adding to an already-established broader body of positive dry-eye trial evidence -- unlike the honestly mixed or contested omega-3 findings already documented for MS and Lupus, this one came out cleanly positive.

**Two real, serious findings push back directly against treating Sjögren's as "just dryness."** A real, meaningfully elevated non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk (roughly 2.7-9.8% of patients over time; more recent, larger studies suggest six-to-nine-fold higher risk than the general population, more reliable than older estimates as high as 44-fold) -- with the real, reassuring context that most of it is a typically slow-growing type. And a real, genuinely striking extraglandular finding: renal tubular acidosis, affecting roughly 5-14% of patients, can cause a real, severe drop in blood potassium leading to sudden muscle weakness or temporary paralysis, and real case reports document this as the FIRST sign of Sjögren's, appearing before the disease's own hallmark dry-eye/dry-mouth symptoms are ever recognized.

**A real, substantial, quantified overlap with two conditions this app already built out**: Sjögren's occurs alongside rheumatoid arthritis in as many as 30% of RA patients in large registries (8.7% by stricter rheumatologist-diagnosed criteria), and alongside lupus in roughly 14-18% of lupus patients per real systematic reviews -- cross-linked directly to `other-rheumatoid-arthritis` and `other-lupus`.

Cross-linked directly to this app's own pre-existing `additive-phosphates` entry, which already covers this same real bioavailability gap from the general-nutrition side.

**Two real, quantified findings from the same trial, reported honestly in opposite directions, anchor this category's own central lesson about how medical guidance actually changes.** The real, large ASCEND trial (15,480 adults with diabetes, no diagnosed cardiovascular disease, 7.4-year follow-up) tested both daily low-dose aspirin and omega-3 supplementation for primary prevention, in the same population, at the same time. Aspirin showed a real, genuine benefit (9.6% to 8.5% serious vascular events) fully counterbalanced by a real, quantified bleeding cost (3.2% to 4.1% major bleeding events) -- converted to concrete numbers, roughly 85 additional vascular events prevented against roughly 90 additional major bleeds caused per 10,000 people treated, the trial's own authors stated plainly that "the absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard." Omega-3 supplementation, tested in the very same trial, produced a real, honest null result (8.9% vs. 9.2% serious vascular events, not statistically significant) -- reported exactly as directly as a positive finding would be, a genuinely more sobering result than omega-3's popular reputation for heart health. Both entries are cross-linked to each other directly, since together they're a real, direct example of why guidance shifts when a large trial's own honest numbers say so, not a reason for distrust.

**The Mediterranean diet's own PREDIMED trial got a genuinely honest treatment of its real 2018 retraction-and-republication story, without inventing an unverified statistic to fill the gap.** The trial's own real design and real correction (randomization irregularities at some study sites led to a formal 2018 retraction of the original 2013 publication, followed by a corrected re-analysis published the same year reaching the same real substantive conclusion) are both confirmed and cited directly -- but the corrected paper's own exact reported hazard ratio could not be independently re-confirmed this session (the abstract fetch cut off before the results section, and two follow-up attempts at a direct primary source both failed), so the entry describes the trial's real design and real retraction story honestly without stating an unverified specific number, consistent with this whole build's standing rule to never fabricate or guess at a citation's exact figures.

**Statins got a real, large, consistent evidence review, directly addressing their commonly debated online reputation**: the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration meta-analysis (14 trials, 90,056 participants) found a real 12% all-cause mortality reduction and 21% major vascular event reduction per 1 mmol/L LDL reduction, with no real increased cancer risk found in the same pooled analysis -- a direct, evidence-based answer to one of the most commonly repeated statin concerns.

**Self-advocacy built in from day one, 2 entries**: real, specific lipid-panel testing intervals by age and sex, with a brief, honestly-scoped mention of apolipoprotein B (apoB) as a real, increasingly discussed concept in cardiology, deliberately without a dedicated citation since a primary apoB source could not be independently re-verified this session -- the concept is presented as real and worth raising by name, not backed by an unverified statistic; and heart attack red flags, including the real, documented pattern that women more often experience atypical symptoms (especially unusual fatigue) rather than classic chest pain, a real, documented reason heart attacks in women are more often missed or delayed.

**2 new `common_medications` rows (atorvastatin, a representative statin; low-dose aspirin) -- lisinopril, losartan, and propranolol were all already present from earlier CKD/Graves' passes and reused directly, since all three are also real, common cardiovascular medications.** 2 new `interaction_rules` rows: `aspirin_ibuprofen_timing` (a real, checkable `timing_separation` rule -- NSAIDs can competitively block aspirin's own irreversible antiplatelet binding if taken too close together, real standard guidance separates the two by several hours) and `atorvastatin_grapefruit_caution` (a real, well-documented, reference-only CYP3A4 interaction, the same pattern already established for `cyclosporine_grapefruit_avoidance`).

Gout is a real, structurally different kind of condition from most already covered: its own strongest evidence is a specific, individually well-studied list of foods and drinks (not one broad dietary pattern), each with its own dedicated large study, giving this category an unusually concrete, food-first character throughout.

**This session's own WebSearch budget was already exhausted before Gout research began** (confirmed via a direct tool-system message, the same exhaustion state already documented for Migraine and Cardiovascular Disease), so every citation here came via the same established `WebFetch`-against-real-pages fallback -- MedlinePlus and StatPearls (both proven reliable throughout this whole build) plus direct PubMed/PMC fetches against real PMIDs. Several citations needed a corrected second search after an initial guessed PMID returned an unrelated paper (a bisphosphonate osteoarthritis trial instead of the coffee/gout study; a lateral-flow-assay methods paper instead of the cherry/gout study) -- both caught immediately by checking the fetched content actually matched the claimed topic before trusting it, rather than assuming a plausible-looking PMID was correct.

**Two real findings from the same landmark 12-year, 47,150-man prospective study anchor this category's own central lesson: not all protein or purine sources carry the same real risk.** Meat carried a real 41% higher gout risk and seafood a real 51% higher risk (highest vs. lowest intake quintile), while dairy carried a real 44% LOWER risk, a genuine protective association from the very same study. The same study's own real, honestly surprising finding: purine-rich vegetables and total protein intake overall were NOT associated with increased risk at all, directly countering the common "all purines are equally risky" assumption. A companion real, large study found sugar-sweetened soft drinks and fructose carrying a real, dose-dependent risk (up to 85% higher at 2+ daily servings) while diet soda showed none, and a third real study found beer carrying the strongest real risk of any alcohol type (49% higher per daily serving) while wine showed no significant association at all -- three separate real "it's not the category, it's the specific thing" findings, each with its own dedicated citation.

**Three individually-tested protective foods each got their own real, dedicated entry.** Cherries: a real case-crossover study found a 35% lower attack risk from cherry intake alone, and a real, striking 75% lower risk when combined with allopurinol, stronger than either alone -- cross-linked directly. Vitamin C: a real, double-blind RCT (184 nonsmokers, 500mg/day for 2 months) found a real, significant uric acid reduction (-0.5 mg/dL vs. +0.09 mg/dL placebo, P<0.0001). Coffee: a real, large study found 6+ daily cups of caffeinated coffee carrying a real 59% lower risk, with decaf also protective (27% lower at 4+ cups) and total caffeine/tea intake showing no effect at all -- real evidence the protective mechanism isn't caffeine itself, cross-linked to this app's own MASLD research, which independently found the same real coffee-protective pattern for a different condition.

**A real, serious medication safety distinction anchors the medications entry**: the real, dedicated CARES safety trial (6,190 patients) comparing the two most common urate-lowering therapies found febuxostat carrying a real 34% higher cardiovascular death risk and 22% higher all-cause mortality risk than allopurinol, despite similar performance on the trial's own broader composite safety measure -- a real, direct reason allopurinol remains the standard first choice, cross-linked to this app's own Cardiovascular Disease research.

**Self-advocacy built in from day one, 2 entries**: HLA-B*58:01 genetic testing before starting allopurinol, with real, specific, named population allele frequencies from the actual 2012 ACR gout guideline's own full text (Han Chinese and Thai individuals ~6-8% regardless of kidney function, Koreans with stage 3+ CKD ~12%, versus ~2% in people of European descent) -- also surfacing the real ACR-recommended serum urate target (<6 mg/dL, or <5 mg/dL for more severe disease); and distinguishing a real gout flare from real septic (infected) arthritis, which can look nearly identical and can genuinely coexist in the same joint, with real guidance to aspirate the joint before a steroid injection when the diagnosis isn't already clear.

Explicitly doesn't contradict this app's own existing, real statin evidence (LDL-lowering itself still shows real mortality benefit, a separate question from what drives LDL up dietarily) -- both stated honestly rather than picking one and ignoring the other.

Found and verified this time: the real INTERHEART study (52 countries, 12,461 cases, 14,637 controls) found the apoB/apoA1 ratio carrying a real, significantly higher population-attributable risk (54%) for heart attack than LDL/HDL (37%) or total cholesterol/HDL (32%), p<0.0001, consistent across ethnicities/sexes/ages. The existing `cvd-lipid-panel-self-advocacy` entry was updated in place to cite this real finding directly and its tier raised from moderate to strong, rather than left with its old "not citing a specific study" caveat now that a real one exists.

**`foodhistory-butter-short-chain-fat`** answers "how well we metabolize butter" directly: butter is a real, natural dietary source of butyrate, the same short-chain fatty acid this app's own Gut & Microbiome research already covers in depth (Treg induction, anti-inflammatory signaling) -- plus a real, classic physiology finding (Nishimura et al. 1996) that short/medium-chain fats are absorbed directly into the portal vein for immediate liver energy use, a genuinely different real pathway from the lymphatic, storage-oriented route most long-chain fats take. Deliberately honest about scope: eating butter isn't a significant therapeutic butyrate source compared to fiber fermentation (still the real, primary source), and this doesn't make butter calorie-free -- the real point is that "all saturated fat behaves identically" was always a chemical oversimplification, not that decades-old guidance was reversed on this specific point.

Also covered the real, settled neural-tube-defect public-health win (600mcg pregnancy / 4-5mg high-risk) and reused the app's own already-cited L-methylfolate/MTHFR-vs-folic-acid data.

**Calcium** (7 entries) surfaced a real, direct thyroid-surgery connection worth naming: postsurgical parathyroid injury (most often during thyroidectomy) accounts for roughly 75% of real hypoparathyroidism cases, with transient post-thyroidectomy hypocalcemia affecting a real 6.9-49% of patients -- cross-linked to Graves' `graves-overview`, since thyroidectomy is a real treatment path there. Hyperthyroidism itself is also a real, documented hypercalcemia cause, the same cross-link working in both directions. Reused the app's own rich, already-cited `supplement_forms`/`nutrient_timing` data (citrate vs. carbonate, the real 500mg single-dose absorption ceiling).

**Potassium** (7 entries) covered both real, dangerous extremes (hypokalemia and hyperkalemia) with their own real, staged ECG progressions, and a real, honest reframing of "just eat a banana": in this app's own database, white beans, avocado, salmon, and sweet potato all carry more potassium per 100g than banana's own real, more modest 358mg/100g. Cross-linked to the existing CKD potassium-restriction and ACE/ARB-monitoring entries, and PCOS's spironolactone caution, rather than re-deriving any of them.

**Vitamin C** (6 entries) covered scurvy as a genuinely still-modern condition (real prevalence from 7.1% in the US to 73.9% in parts of northern India, not a historical curiosity), a real, narrow toxicity risk concentrated almost entirely in kidney-stone-prone men, and a real, distinctive dose-dependent absorption mechanism (efficient to ~100mg/day, dropping to 50% or less above 1,500mg in one dose) -- the identical single-dose-ceiling pattern already established for calcium, named directly as a recurring theme across this whole series rather than a coincidence. **Prostate Health added as this app's nineteenth real condition, 2026-08-08, same day, direct question: "Is there any solid reason for prostate health to be included related to food health and gut microbiome and whole foods?"** Researched directly before deciding, not assumed from the premise alone -- and the real evidence answered yes, decisively. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is genuinely one of the most common conditions in aging men, real data confirming 29% prevalence in men in their 50s, climbing to 44.7% in their 60s, 58.1% in their 70s, and 69.2% at 80+; prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in American men (~27% of new male cancer diagnoses). The gut-microbiome connection is real and specific, not a stretch to include here: a real systematic review found gut dysbiosis (an elevated Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio, real shifts in Prevotella/Ruminococcus/Lactobacillus abundance) directly linked to BPH through the same SCFA-production/systemic-inflammation mechanism this app's own Gut & Microbiome research already documents for autoimmune disease; specific Ruminococcus strains can directly convert hormone precursors into androgens inside the gut, with real, documented worse prognosis in castrate-resistant prostate cancer patients carrying more of it; and a real, large, 22-year study (47,896 men) found the highest quintile of dietary choline intake carried a 70% higher risk of lethal prostate cancer, mediated by gut bacteria converting choline into TMAO.

Added to the `conditions` reference table (`prostate_health`, non_autoimmune, sort_order 19, status `in_progress`) -- Profile's own condition picker already reads this table dynamically, so no app-code change was needed for it to appear there. Psoriasis's real, genuinely mixed 40-60%-improve/10-20%-worsen pregnancy split plus real biologic-safety data; Graves' real, counterintuitive finding that a mother's own TRAb can cause fetal thyrotoxicosis even after SHE has become hypothyroid from past treatment; T1D's real, tighter pregnancy glucose targets and the real, quantified stakes of falling short of them; Celiac's real 8.9-fold miscarriage risk that fully reverses on a gluten-free diet; IBD's real finding that remission AT CONCEPTION, not just during pregnancy, is the single biggest predictor of a healthy outcome; MS's real, dramatic 70%-relapse-reduction-then-postpartum-doubling swing; Lupus's real anti-Ro/anti-La congenital-heart-block risk; Sjögren's own real, quantified version of that same antibody risk, 1-2% baseline jumping to 17-18% after one affected pregnancy; Real findings added: **CVD** -- a coronary artery calcium score of zero is real, useful risk-stratification information, but a large MESA analysis found it has a real "warranty period" (3-7 years, shorter with diabetes), not a lifetime guarantee (PMID 33129734); losartan's real, mechanistically distinct uricosuric effect (URAT1 transporter inhibition) that the rest of its own ARB drug class doesn't share (PMID 18670416). **IBD** -- the real SONIC trial (Colombel et al. 2010, PMID 20393175), showing combination biologic-plus-immunomodulator therapy beating either drug alone by a real, wide margin; the Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet's real randomized-trial evidence (PMID 31170412) as a genuinely more sustainable whole-food alternative to exclusive enteral nutrition. **Lupus** -- neuropsychiatric lupus's real, underrecognized 30-40% prevalence, with cognitive dysfunction alone near 38% (PMC11227614); anifrolumab, a real, mechanistically distinct newer biologic (blocking type I interferon rather than B cells) with real TULIP-2 trial data (47.8% vs. 31.5% response, PMID 31851795). **Migraine** -- gepants (ubrogepant/rimegepant), a real newer acute-treatment class working through the same CGRP pathway as this app's own preventive-medication research, with real ACHIEVE II trial data (PMID 31742631) and a real, lower medication-overuse-headache risk than triptans; FDA-cleared neuromodulation devices (Cefaly's real PREMICE trial, PMID 23390177; gammaCore's real PRESTO trial, PMID 29907608) as a genuinely drug-free option. **PCOS** -- GLP-1 medications (semaglutide/liraglutide) moving into real PCOS trials, working through the same insulin-resistance mechanism this condition is built on, with a real trial finding menstrual-cycle restoration in 86.87% of participants on combination therapy; anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) as a real, increasingly-used blood-test complement to the ultrasound-based Rotterdam diagnostic criterion, with real pooled sensitivity/specificity data (79%/87%, PMID 38944177). **Psoriasis** -- IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab) as a real, newer, more targeted biologic class, with real VOYAGE 1 trial data showing 73.3% reaching PASI 90 versus 2.9% on placebo, and a real, growing advantage over an older biologic through a full year of treatment; the Koebner phenomenon, a real, named, well-documented pattern where physical skin trauma itself triggers a genuinely new psoriasis patch. **Sjögren's** -- rituximab's real, honest negative primary-trial result (the TEARS trial, PMID 24727841), a genuine example of biologically plausible treatment not translating into the specific symptom improvement a randomized trial is built to detect; oral candidiasis as a real, common, treatable consequence of Sjögren's own dry-mouth mechanism, distinct from the dental-caries risk already covered. **Type 1 Diabetes** -- autoimmune thyroid disease as the single most common real comorbidity riding alongside T1D (PMID 37303388), with real, current screening guidance (TPO antibodies and TSH at diagnosis, annual TSH thereafter in antibody-positive patients); continuous glucose monitoring alone, without a full automated insulin-delivery system, already producing a real, measurable clinical benefit on its own (the DIAMOND trial, PMID 28118453).

**Every group of entries within a Digest section now sorts in a real, deterministic order, 2026-08-08, direct correction: "there seems to be a randomness to how the data within each Digest area are being listed from start to finish or which other information is next to them. There needs to be an order to sorting applied to the group of each area so even if the users just decides to scroll around and look at random things it should all track in a logical order in each section."** Confirmed the real root cause before fixing: every group's own entry order (a Basic Health topic/subtopic leaf list, a condition's own pillar shelf) had always just reflected the literal order entries were WRITTEN into the source file across many separate build passes over many days, not any real reading order, so scrolling through genuinely did feel arbitrary. Real findings added: **Celiac** -- a real, direct pediatric-vs-adult comparison (classic GI symptoms in 79% of children vs. just 14% of adults; even the lab/biopsy findings themselves differ by age, PMID 26506381). **CKD** -- the real, still-unsettled age-adapted-eGFR debate (a real 1.5-million-person European cohort finding most healthy 65-year-olds already score below the standard CKD threshold, real evidence behind arguments that CKD is overdiagnosed in older adults). **MASLD** -- real, current pediatric prevalence data (7.4% general pediatric population, 52.5% in children with obesity specifically, PMID 41230444), MASLD now the most common chronic pediatric liver disease. **Graves'** -- real, pooled pediatric remission-rate data (15.5% under 2 years of treatment, rising to 33.0% past 5 years, PMID 39501471), a real, evidence-backed reason to extend treatment duration in children well past what an adult protocol would suggest. **IBS** -- real, pediatric-specific Rome IV criteria and prevalence (~22% of children, PMID 34768604), including a real fourth subtype (abdominal migraine) with no adult equivalent. **MS** -- a real, striking, almost paradoxical pediatric-onset finding (2.75x higher relapse rate than adults, yet 20 years to reach a disability milestone adults reach in 8, PMID 27572865). **Prostate Health** -- the real, foundational age-specific PSA reference-range study (PMID 7541586), a "normal" PSA climbing from 2.5 in someone's 40s to 6.5 in their 70s. **Rheumatoid Arthritis** -- elderly-onset RA (EORA) as a real, distinct clinical entity (larger-joint involvement, a flu-like onset resembling polymyalgia rheumatica in a real 4x-more-common pattern, yet a real more aggressive disease course despite similar starting activity, PMID 39913010). **Type 2 Diabetes** -- the real, landmark TODAY2 follow-up finding youth-onset T2D genuinely more aggressive than adult-onset (60% with a real complication within 15 years, most still in their 20s, a real 3x-higher cardiovascular event rate than an older comparison population, PMID 34320286).

**Age content extended across the remaining 9 conditions, plus a first dedicated Hashimoto's age entry, plus a real, meaningful expansion of the functional age-rules engine, 2026-08-08, same day, direct request: "Continue the volumetric-depth-push with the next-lowest-count conditions, and then make sure all age related things get applied to all 19 conditions extensively."** Checked directly which conditions still lacked a dedicated age-focused entry (the previous batch had covered 9 of the 18 non-Hashimoto's conditions plus none of Hashimoto's own) -- Cardiovascular Disease, Gout, IBD, Lupus, Migraine, PCOS, Psoriasis, Sjögren's, and Type 1 Diabetes were the real gap, plus Hashimoto's itself, which had only ever had passing, incidental age mentions (organSystems.ts's overtreatment/fracture entry, the 1924 iodization history entry, seronegative Hashimoto's) inside entries whose main topic was something else, never a real, standalone age-focused entry of its own.

Real, independently-verified findings, one per condition: **CVD** -- silent or atypical heart attacks make up over 60% of cases in adults over 60, presenting as confusion, weakness, or a fall rather than chest pain, with autopsy data finding correct diagnosis made in life in fewer than half of elderly cases (PMID 24714791). **Gout** -- early-onset gout (before 40) traces disproportionately to real, identifiable genetic causes (UMOD-gene kidney disease, ABCG2 transporter dysfunction) rather than diet alone, the opposite of gout's usual "disease of aging" framing. **IBD** -- elderly-onset IBD looks genuinely different (left-sided colitis, colonic-predominant Crohn's) and takes roughly 3x longer to diagnose (up to 6 years vs. 2) than younger-onset disease, with a real 51%-vs-39% initial-misdiagnosis-rate gap. **Lupus** -- late-onset lupus (50+, 20% of all cases) is a real, measurably milder disease, lower SLEDAI scores, less classic rash, less kidney involvement, but genuinely easy to mistake for ordinary aging or osteoarthritis. **Migraine** -- migraine frequency genuinely shifts around menopause (a real, honest 24.4%-improved-vs-35.7%-worsened split), but a brand-new headache starting after 50 always warrants real evaluation to rule out a vascular or structural cause, distinct from an existing pattern simply changing. **PCOS** -- real, age-adjusted diagnostic criteria exist specifically because normal post-menarche cycle irregularity (75% of teens, 21-45-day cycles in year one) is nearly indistinguishable from PCOS-related irregularity for the first 2-3 years. **Psoriasis** -- guttate psoriasis, a real, distinct drop-shaped-lesion pattern, is the second most common pediatric psoriasis form and follows a real streptococcal infection in up to 80% of cases. **Sjögren's** -- dryness, fatigue, and joint pain overlap so closely with normal aging that diagnosis in older patients is real and disproportionately delayed, illustrated by a real documented case of a year of untreated symptoms attributed to age alone. **Type 1 Diabetes** -- LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes in adults), a real, slower-progressing autoimmune form diagnosed in adulthood, may account for 4-14% of everyone currently labeled type 2, with real, concrete stakes to misdiagnosis. **Hashimoto's** -- a new `labs-age-adjusted-tsh-target-older-adults` entry (`lib/digest/labsMedication.ts`) covers the real, often-missed fact that the TSH TARGET itself is supposed to rise with age (real thyroid-society guidance: 4-6 mIU/L for ages 70-80, versus a younger-adult target), directly connecting to this app's own already-existing overtreatment-risk entry (`organ-overtreatment-bone-heart-risk`) and TSH-range-debate entry (`advocacy-tsh-optimal-range-debate`), both updated with reciprocal cross-links.

**Global Perspective: the first real batch of international/regional Digest content, 2026-08-08, same day, direct implementation of the "International scope" architecture decision recorded above.** One dedicated, independently-verified "Global Perspective" entry added to every one of the 19 conditions (Hashimoto's + all 18 others), each covering both real, cited international prevalence variation AND the real, corroborating explanation for why -- genetics, diet, environment, latitude, industrialization, or healthcare/screening access -- matching exactly the format named directly in the request ("Provide the corroborating evidence for the reasons they are having these problems in their countries").

Real findings added, one per condition: **Hashimoto's** -- China's own national salt-iodization program, tracked across three regions with different iodine intake, found autoimmune thyroiditis prevalence rising step by step alongside iodine intake (up to 16.1% in some Chinese populations), a real, direct dose-response demonstration of this app's own already-covered two-edged-iodine research at true national scale. **RA** -- Indigenous populations of the Americas (Pima 5.3%, Chippewa 6.8%, Qom of Argentina among the highest reported worldwide) carry real RA prevalence 5-6x the global average, tied to a specific real genetic marker (HLA-DRB1*1402), against consistently lower rates in China, Japan, and rural Africa. **Psoriasis** -- a real, stark latitude gradient: Norway 3.8-4.6% prevalence vs. East Asia's 0.14%, tied to both latitude/UV exposure and Caucasian ancestry specifically. **Graves' Disease** -- a real, classic Denmark-vs-Iceland comparative study found Graves' more than twice as common in young people in iodine-sufficient Iceland vs. iodine-deficient Denmark, while overall thyrotoxicosis (driven by nodular goiter) ran the opposite direction -- real, direct evidence that iodine status shapes WHICH thyroid disease shows up, not just how much thyroid disease overall. **Type 1 Diabetes** -- Finland's real, world-highest T1D incidence (64.2/100,000 in 2005) against Japan (2.25-2.37/100,000) and China (as low as 0.1/100,000), a 25-600x real gap, with a real six-fold gradient found at the Finland/Russian Karelia border despite identical HLA frequencies -- strong, direct evidence for environmental rather than purely genetic causation. **Celiac Disease** -- Western Sahara's Saharawi population (5.6% prevalence, among the highest ever documented) tied to real, very high HLA-DQ2 frequency, against East Asia's 0.06% seroprevalence and DQ2's near-total absence in Japan. **IBD** -- real projections showing India's IBD prevalence quadrupling by 2035, tied directly to documented dietary Westernization, urbanization, and hygiene changes in newly industrializing regions. **Multiple Sclerosis** -- the real, classic latitude gradient (up to 10x prevalence increase from equator to 60°N/S), with real migration-study evidence that residence before age 15, not current residence, sets someone's real underlying risk. **Lupus** -- real, quantified ethnicity-based severity gaps, not just prevalence differences (lupus nephritis rates: African American 59.69/100,000, Asian 56.56/100,000, White 15.83/100,000; real hazard ratios for nephritis up to 4.3x by ethnicity). **Sjögren's** -- real geographic (Mediterranean vs. Northern Europe) and ethnic variation in both prevalence AND presentation itself (female-to-male ratio 27:1 in Asian patients vs. 7:1 in Black/African-American patients; diagnosis 7 years earlier on average in Black/African-American patients). **PCOS** -- South Asian women's real, higher PCOS prevalence and the "Asian Indian phenotype" (greater visceral fat, lower muscle mass at the same body weight, driving insulin resistance at lower BMI). **CKD** -- CKDu, a real, distinct kidney disease epidemic in Central American sugarcane workers and Sri Lankan farmers, occurring WITHOUT diabetes, hypertension, or glomerulonephritis, tied to real heat stress/dehydration/agrochemical exposure. **MASLD** -- real regional prevalence swings (Latin America 44.4% vs. Western Europe 25.1%; South Asia up to 60% in diabetic subgroups) tied partly to the real PNPLA3 gene variant's uneven distribution by ancestry (explaining Hispanic populations' higher US MASLD/MASH rates). **Type 2 Diabetes** -- Nauru's real, world-highest T2D prevalence (~50% of adults), tied to a documented multi-decade dietary shift and the real "thrifty gene" hypothesis, plus South Asians' real lower-BMI diabetes-risk threshold. **IBS** -- an honest, real complication: pooled prevalence swings from 9.2% (Rome III criteria) to 3.8% (Rome IV criteria) in the same global literature, meaning much of the apparent regional gap (Western 20% vs. South Asia/Middle East 7-10%) may reflect diagnostic-criteria translation issues as much as true biological difference -- tiered moderate specifically for this honesty. **Migraine** -- real global burden data (1.2 billion people affected) showing the highest disability burden in sub-Saharan Africa not because migraine itself is more common there, but because of real, documented limited access to effective treatment. **Cardiovascular Disease** -- the real, foundational Seven Countries Study (southern Europe 2-10% prevalence vs. northern Europe 10-18%), the original evidence behind this app's own Mediterranean-diet research, with a real note that CVD burden is now shifting toward low/middle-income countries as diets Westernize. **Gout** -- Oceania's real, world-highest gout prevalence (Māori, Pacific Islander, Taiwanese Aboriginal populations), tied to a real, well-characterized genetic urate-transporter variant (SLC2A9/GLUT9) reducing kidney urate clearance. **Prostate Health** -- a real, striking migrant-study finding (Japanese men in the US developing prostate cancer at 4-5x the rate of men in Japan; Shanghai-to-California migrants seeing a 12-fold rise) -- among the strongest real evidence in oncology that diet/environment, not genetics, drives most of the 30-fold regional incidence gap.

Every claim independently verified via WebSearch before being written in. Real findings: Cassia cinnamon (what "cinnamon" almost always means on a grocery shelf) can carry over 100x the coumarin of true Ceylon cinnamon (2,650-7,017 mg/kg vs. negligible, against a real EFSA tolerable daily intake limit); a European Commission survey suspected 46% of 147 honey samples of sugar-syrup adulteration; saffron adulteration runs a real 20-43% depending on the market surveyed; Oceana's DNA testing found 33% of 1,215 US seafood samples mislabeled (snapper 87%, tuna 59%); the FDA names maple syrup directly as a real economically-motivated-adulteration target; and USDA's own "natural" label says nothing about how an animal was raised, while "grass-fed" can legally describe an animal grain-finished in its final months, verified by a farmer's own signed affidavit rather than independent audit. **A real, deliberate honesty correction included rather than the more dramatic popular version**: the widely repeated "most olive oil is fake" claim, usually pointing to the UC Davis Olive Center study, does not hold up as stated -- that study found most failed oils were genuinely 100% olive oil that failed a sensory/freshness grading standard (should have been labeled Virgin or Refined, not Extra Virgin), not oil cut with cheaper seed or vegetable oil, and this topic reports that more precise, less dramatic finding rather than the inaccurate popular one.

Two new bundled reference-database tables, `curated_recipes`/`curated_recipe_ingredients` (patched directly into `assets/data/foods_reference.db` via `sqlite3.exe`, the same established workaround for this session's continued lack of a Python interpreter) -- app-authored content, deliberately NOT written into the user's own local `favorites` table, since these aren't something a person created and shouldn't be mixed into or deletable from their own real favorites list. A real, deliberate design choice worth naming: each ingredient row stores a plain `(category, base_name)` pair, never a hardcoded numeric `food_id` -- a future reference-database rebuild can renumber ids, and a recipe built on a stored id could silently point at the wrong row (or nothing) afterward. New `getCuratedRecipe(id)` (`lib/db.ts`) resolves each ingredient to a real, CURRENT `food_id`/`source` at read time instead, the same "base_name is the stable identity" discipline this whole reference database already runs on.

Every one of the 70 real ingredient rows across all 12 recipes was independently confirmed to have at least one visible reference-database row before being written in, so this final fallback is a real, exercised safety net for the "not Raw, not untagged" case, not a guess that happens to work.
